questions.title: A split-server benchmark that counted empty answers
questions.prompt:
A team split Qwen/Qwen3-8B into a prefill server and a decode server on two L4s over TCP, ran the open-loop benchmark through the router at 8 requests per second, and posted the result as a win: 751.85 tokens of output per second, against 728.61 for the single FP8 server at the same rate. Here are lines from the prefill log, the decode log and the benchmark summary. Read them and tell me what you see.

```text
… Decode batch, #running-req: 2, #token: 1206, token usage: 0.41, pre-allocated usage: 0.00, #prealloc-req: 19, #transfer-req: 0, #retracted-req: 0
… TCP lane queue-full rejection count: 4096
… Session 151.242.195.41:15367 failed.
Prefill transfer failed lines: 2902
Successful requests:                     240
Total generated tokens (retokenized):    0
Mean TTFT (ms):                          0.00
```
questions.short: The run produced no text. Every request counted as a success through the router, but zero tokens came back when the client retokenized the output, and a mean first-token time of 0.00 ms is not a measurement. The decode log shows why: the decode copy could run only 2 requests while 19 waited for memory, prefill kept producing KV for them, the TCP transfer queue to decode filled and rejected 4096 times, the session failed, and 2902 later transfers failed with it, so the 751.85 figure is the speed at which the router returned empty answers.
questions.full:
### Read the lines in order

1. `#running-req: 2` with `#prealloc-req: 19` at a token usage of 0.41. The decode side runs two requests and 19 more wait for decode memory. That pool is small: the decode server sat on the shared card with 2,925 tokens, against 24,094 on the prefill card.
2. `TCP lane queue-full rejection count: 4096`. Prefill kept producing KV caches for requests that decode could not take, and the transfer queue to decode filled.
3. `Session ... failed.` Three minutes into the sweep the transfer session died, and it did not come back.
4. `Prefill transfer failed lines: 2902`. Every later request failed its transfer.
5. `Successful requests: 240` with `Total generated tokens (retokenized): 0` and `Mean TTFT (ms): 0.00`. Each failed request still returned HTTP 200 through the router, with no text.

### Why the summary lied

The client counts a success on the status code. The throughput line counts the tokens the client asked for, 128 per request with the end token ignored, not the tokens it received. Only two numbers gave the run away: the retokenized output tokens, which count what came back, and a first-token time of zero, which no real request can have. The manual did not publish the throughput figure, and its kit now refuses a run in which every request has a TTFT of 0.

### The swapped split

The team then put decode on the card with the full pool of 24,094 tokens and prefill on the shared card with 2,925. From 1 to 8 users every request came back with text. At 16 users only 2,048 of 8,192 generated tokens came back as text. At 32 users every request came back empty, and the kit stopped the sweep. The original direction failed earlier: at 2 users only 512 of 2,048 generated tokens came back, and at 4 users none did. The manual's conclusion is that it has no measured result for the split under load on this pair of cards, and it does not claim one.

### The rule

Check `Total generated tokens (retokenized)` against `Total generated tokens` in every disaggregated benchmark before you read its throughput, and look at the TTFT distribution for values that cannot be real. In production, watch the bootstrap-failed and transfer-failed counters, the transfer latency and speed, and the decode pre-allocation and transfer queue gauges.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Which two numbers in such a summary must you read before the throughput? Expected: the retokenized output tokens against the generated tokens, and the TTFT distribution; a gap between the two token counts or a first token of zero means requests returned without text.
- **Level 4:** Why did the decode pool fill while prefill kept working? Expected: the decode copy sat on the shared card with a pool of 2,925 tokens, so it ran 2 requests and 19 waited for memory; prefill had 24,094 tokens and kept producing KV for them, so the transfer queue to decode filled and the session died.
- **Level 4:** The swapped split served text up to 8 users and lost it at 16 and 32. What does that say about the pair? Expected: the small side limits the pair whichever role it has; with prefill on the small card, 2,048 of 8,192 generated tokens came back at 16 users and none at 32, so there is no measured result for this pair under load, and the honest report says so.
questions.wrong:
- "240 of 240 requests succeeded, so the system is healthy." The router returned HTTP 200 with no text for every failed request; zero retokenized tokens and a first token of 0.00 ms show that nothing was generated.
- "751.85 beats 728.61, so disaggregation won." The figure counts tokens the client asked for, not tokens it received; the manual did not publish it, and its kit now refuses a run in which every request has a TTFT of 0.
- "The TCP backend is the problem, so use RDMA." The queue filled because decode could not take the KV: it ran 2 requests with 19 waiting for memory on a pool of 2,925 tokens; a faster link does not add memory to the decode side.
- "Retries would have fixed the failed transfers." The session failed three minutes in and did not come back, so every later transfer failed; the fix is a decode pool that can hold the requests and a check that the output exists.

questions.title: An admission cap decides who waits
questions.prompt: At 32 concurrent users your L4 chat service streams badly: the P99 inter-token gap is 613 ms, and your target is 100 ms or less per token with a first token within 1 second. A teammate proposes `--max-num-seqs 16` so that each step holds fewer requests. What do you expect, and what does the measurement say?
questions.short: A cap does not make room for more users; it only chooses who waits. With the cap at 16 and 32 users, each stream got a little smoother, a median ITL of 69.8 against 80.5 ms and a P99 ITL of 595 against 613, but half the users waited in the queue, the median first token went from 1.8 to 12.3 s, and output fell 38 percent to 171.8 tokens per second. At 64 users no cap that the manual tried brought the P99 ITL under 1.1 s, so the fix on this card is fewer users per replica, not a cap.
questions.full:
### Where the stream broke

Qwen/Qwen3-8B on the L4 in the full-clock session, 512 prompt tokens and 128 output tokens, three seeds:

| Users | Output tok/s | Median TTFT | P99 ITL | Met the target | Median SM clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 112.8 | 0.25 s | 67 ms | 75% | 1,485 MHz |
| 16 | 201.3 | 0.29 s | 85 ms | 64% | 1,455 MHz |
| 32 | 275.1 | 1.80 s | 613 ms | 0% | 1,275 MHz |
| 64 | 242.3 | 11.18 s | 1,233 ms | 0% | 1,005 MHz |

This sweep did not reset the prefix cache, so the rows below 32 users read too well; with a reset the share that met the target at 16 users fell to 25 percent and the P99 ITL there was 522 ms. Each step on this GPU has a budget of 2,048 tokens, and new prompt chunks share the step with the running streams, so the streams pause.

### The cap at 32 users

| Config | Output tok/s | Median TTFT | Median ITL | P99 ITL | Median SM clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| default, 256 | 275.1 | 1.8 s | 80.5 ms | 613 ms | 1,275 MHz |
| `--max-num-seqs 16` | 171.8 | 12.3 s | 69.8 ms | 595 ms | 1,365 MHz |

The cap run had the higher clock, so the clock does not explain the loss. The stream got a little smoother, half the users waited for their first token, and output fell by 38 percent.

### Caps at 64 users

With the clock locked at 900 MHz, two seeds and a reset per run, against SGLang on the same card:

| Config | Median TTFT | P99 ITL | Output tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| SGLang default | 19.4 s | 143 to 153 ms | 225 to 231 |
| vLLM default | 11.8 s | 1,359 ms | 220 |
| `--max-num-seqs 32` | 17.2 to 20.6 s | 1,163 to 1,399 ms | 196 to 230 |
| `--max-num-active-seqs 48` | 11.8 s | 1,329 to 1,373 ms | 215 to 218 |
| `--max-num-active-seqs 16` | 44.8 to 48.8 s | 1,133 to 1,139 ms | 129 to 136 |

No cap brought the vLLM P99 ITL near the SGLang value. At 16 or 32 running requests the P99 ITL stayed above 1.1 s and the first token waited 17 to 65 s. On this card a cap does not fix the long gaps at 64 users. Fewer users per replica does.

### The small pool is the other queue

A pool of 6,560 tokens against 24,096 at 32 users gave a median time to first token of 31.6 s against 3.1 s and a P99 first token of 48.0 against 7.1 s. A request of 640 tokens needs 640 tokens of pool by its end, so about 10 requests fit in the small pool and the other 22 waited for a running request to finish. The small-pool run also fell to 248 MHz, but a clock 3.6 times lower cannot explain a first token 10 times later; the queue did.

### How SGLang admits, and why a queue is the honest failure

SGLang admits a request only when a forecast fits the pool. A new request must fit its uncached prompt tokens plus its remaining `max_new_tokens`, clipped to 4,096. Each running request holds back its remaining `max_new_tokens` times a ratio that starts at 0.7 and falls to 0.098 over 600 decode steps, because most requests stop early. When the forecast is too bold, the scheduler retracts running requests to the queue and they prefill again. In a small pool of 4,096 tokens with 16 users asking for 512 tokens each, exactly five requests ran at a time: each token took 24 ms once a request started, and the median user waited 27.9 s for the first token. Every request succeeded. A long queue with fast tokens is admission control doing its job; a retraction is the alarm, and more than about one per minute is a configuration bug. Set realistic `max_new_tokens` in clients: a client that asks for 4,096 tokens and uses 200 makes the reservation of every new request about 20 times too big.

### What to do

1. Set the targets for the first token and the time per token.
2. Sweep users with a reset per run, and find the last count that meets both.
3. If the cache usage is near full and requests wait, the pool is too small: add room with an FP8 cache or FP8 weights.
4. If the pool has room and the P99 ITL is too high, the GPU is full: add a GPU or a replica, and enforce the knee in the client or the gateway.
5. Read the P99 ITL when you pick an engine for chat. On the GB10 the two engines gave the same output at 32 and 64 users, and the vLLM P99 ITL was 478 against 220 ms at 32 users.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** The cap run had a higher clock than the default run. Why does that matter for the conclusion? Expected: a higher clock should help the cap run, so the clock does not explain its 38 percent lower output; the loss belongs to the cap.
- **Level 3:** How does SGLang decide to admit a request, and what happens when its forecast is wrong? Expected: a new request must fit its uncached prompt plus its remaining max_new_tokens, and running requests hold back their remaining output times a ratio that starts at 0.7 and falls to 0.098 over 600 decode steps; when the forecast is too bold the scheduler retracts running requests to the queue and they prefill again.
- **Level 4:** The pool has room, the tail gap is still over target, and a cap only moves the wait. What is left? Expected: the GPU is full; add a GPU or a replica and put fewer users on each, enforce the knee in the client or the gateway, and read the P99 ITL when you pick an engine, because at the same output the two engines differed about twofold on the GB10.
questions.wrong:
- "A cap on running requests makes room for more users." It only chooses who waits; at 32 users the cap of 16 moved the wait into the queue, with the first token at 12.3 s, and cost 38 percent of the output.
- "Lower the maximum model length to help the queue." The pool stays the same size, so it does not help when the cache usage is near full; add room with an FP8 cache or FP8 weights.
- "Clients should ask for a large max_new_tokens to be safe." The admission forecast reserves it; a client that asks for 4,096 tokens and uses 200 makes the reservation of every new request about 20 times too big, so fewer requests are admitted.
- "A queue means the server is broken." A long queue with fast tokens is admission control doing its job; the five admitted requests in the small-pool run got 24 ms per token while the median user waited 27.9 s, and a retraction, not a queue, is the alarm.

questions.title: Acceptance by draft position, tokens per pass
questions.prompt: A vLLM server runs Qwen/Qwen3-8B with an EAGLE3 draft of depth 3. Over a run of answers near 2,000 tokens at 8 users, the counters show that the draft at position one was accepted with probability 0.77, position two with 0.54, and position three with 0.38. Estimate the mean number of tokens that one verify pass commits, and say what you would check before you rely on that gain for long answers.
questions.short: Each verify pass commits the accepted drafts plus one bonus token from the target, so the mean acceptance length is one plus the sum of the per-position acceptance rates. With 0.77, 0.54 and 0.38 that is about 2.69 tokens per pass, which is the value vLLM reported on GSM8K in that run. Before I trust it on long answers I would read the acceptance of the longest answers alone, with real output lengths and without ignore-eos, because another study saw the acceptance fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5 on answers that ran toward 20,000 tokens.
questions.full:
### The arithmetic

The per-position rates already include the order of the chain: position two can only be accepted when position one was, and 0.54 is the share of all passes in which position two was accepted. The expected number of accepted drafts is the sum of the rates, and the target always adds one token of its own, so:

```text
mean acceptance length = 1 + 0.77 + 0.54 + 0.38 = 2.69
```

On ShareGPT the same run gave 0.67, 0.42 and 0.26, which is 2.35. Both match the mean acceptance length that vLLM reported from its counters.

### What the manual measured on long answers

Qwen/Qwen3-8B in BF16 at 8 users, answers up to 2,048 tokens, no ignore-eos, median answer 1,800 to 2,000 tokens:

| Engine | Dataset | Mean acceptance length | Accepted per draft position 1 / 2 / 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| SGLang EAGLE3 | GSM8K | 2.68 | |
| SGLang EAGLE3 | ShareGPT | 2.32 | |
| vLLM EAGLE3 | GSM8K | 2.69 | 0.77 / 0.54 / 0.38 |
| vLLM EAGLE3 | ShareGPT | 2.35 | 0.67 / 0.42 / 0.26 |

On short 128-token answers in the same session, SGLang gave 2.69 to 2.78 on GSM8K and 2.33 to 2.43 on ShareGPT. Its long answers stayed within 0.01 of those ranges.

### By position inside the answer

A second test ran 8 prompts with thinking on, greedy, at one user, up to 4,096 tokens, and read the acceptance in segments:

| Segment of the output | SGLang | vLLM |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 256 | 2.05 to 2.64 (8) | 2.14 to 2.51 (8) |
| 256 to 512 | 1.95 to 2.64 (8) | 2.09 to 2.55 (8) |
| 512 to 1,024 | 2.11 to 2.77 (8) | 2.12 to 2.79 (8) |
| 1,024 to 2,048 | 2.09 to 2.47 (5) | 1.72 to 2.66 (5) |
| 2,048 to 4,096 | 2.33 and 2.48 (2) | 2.35 and 2.60 (2) |

Up to 4,096 tokens the acceptance did not fall steadily. Only 2 of the 8 prompts ran past 2,048 tokens, so the last segment rests on two answers, and the limit of 4,096 came from the memory on that GPU. So the test did not reach the range of the study that saw the fall.

### When acceptance does fall

One incident shows a different cause. A draft config with 2,048 positions and no rope scaling accepted 3.2 tokens at 1k input tokens, 1.6 at 3k and 1.2 at 10k. At 10k the server produced 63.9 tokens per second against 102.7 without speculation. The draft could not read past its position limit. Adding the rope scaling and 131,072 positions to the draft config fixed it. The override variable that skips the context check removes the check and does not teach the draft to read long prompts.

### What to read

- vLLM: `spec_decode_num_draft_tokens` and `spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens` from `/metrics`, and the `SpecDecoding metrics` line in the log.
- SGLang: `accept len` and `accept rate` on each decode log line, `sglang:spec_accept_length` from `/metrics`, and `spec_accept_length` in the `meta_info` of each `/generate` response, which gives you the value per answer.
- Compare the P99 ITL and the P99 TTFT with and without the draft, and compare `max_position_embeddings` of the draft with your longest prompts.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why is the bonus token always there? Expected: the target computes a distribution one position past the last accepted draft, so even when every draft is rejected the pass still writes one token of its own, as plain decoding would.
- **Level 3:** The ShareGPT rates were 0.67, 0.42 and 0.26. What length do you get, and why is it below GSM8K? Expected: 2.35; open chat is harder for the draft to predict than math steps and code, so fewer drafts match the target.
- **Level 4:** Acceptance was 3.2 at 1k input tokens and 1.2 at 10k on a draft with 2,048 positions. Cause and fix? Expected: the draft could not read past its position limit, so its guesses degrade with the prompt length; the rope scaling and the longer position count in the draft config fixed it, and the override variable only removes the check.
questions.wrong:
- "The mean acceptance length is the mean of the three rates." It is the expected count of accepted drafts, the sum of the rates, plus the bonus token; 0.77 plus 0.54 plus 0.38 plus one is 2.69, not a value below one.
- "An acceptance length of 2.69 means 2.69 times the speed." Each pass also pays the draft steps and the check; on the L4 the dense model gave each token 1.6 to 2.3 times faster and no more output from 32 users, because the draft took pool space.
- "A long answer keeps the acceptance of a short one." In the manual's own test to 4,096 tokens it did, but another study saw it fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5 toward 20,000 tokens, and a draft with too few positions fell from 3.2 to 1.2 with the prompt length; read your own long answers.

questions.title: Design a chat service on a fleet of L4 cards
questions.prompt: Design the serving layer for a chat product on a fleet of L4 cards with Qwen/Qwen3-8B. The target is a first token within 1 second and 100 ms or less per token for the P99 user. Every request shares a 2,048-token system prompt, and sessions run for several turns. How many users per card, which precision, which caps, and what do you measure before launch?
questions.short: Size from the pool and the knee, not from throughput. In BF16 the 24,094-token pool on an L4 holds about 37 requests of 640 tokens, and with a cache reset the P99 gap between tokens at 16 users was already 522 ms, so a BF16 replica meets the target for well under 16 users; the FP8 checkpoint with an FP8 cache grows the pool to 142,369 tokens and served 2.87 requests per second within the same target at 64 users, where BF16 served none. So I would serve FP8 after an accuracy check on our prompts, put the shared system prompt first so that the cache holds it, keep the pool large enough for the sessions that return, cap users per replica at the measured knee in the gateway, and run the sweep with a flush, a clock record and a mixed length distribution before launch.
questions.full:
### Users per card

The knee on an L4 in BF16 sits between 8 and 16 users once the prefix cache is reset before each run. With the reset, 50 percent of requests met the target at 8 users against 75 to 81 percent without it, and at 16 users the share fell from about 65 percent to 25 percent, with a P99 ITL of 522 ms against 82 to 84 ms unflushed. The median first token with the reset was about 650 ms at 4 users, 951 to 978 ms at 8, and 1,550 to 1,587 ms at 16. Under a fixed arrival rate, both precisions met the target for every request up to 1 request per second; BF16 held 0.88 requests per second within target at 2 offered and none from 4, while FP8 held 3.18 at 4 offered. So a BF16 replica carries a handful of chat users, and an FP8 replica several times more; the sweep decides the exact count.

### Precision

On the same L4 the FP8 checkpoint with an FP8 cache changed the shape of the whole curve:

| Concurrency | BF16 output tok/s | FP8 output tok/s | BF16 median TTFT | FP8 median TTFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 13.42 | 24.53 | 189.16 ms | 140.72 ms |
| 16 | 201.09 | 313.92 | 211.78 ms | 147.52 ms |
| 32 | 270.11 | 507.20 | 2,969.61 ms | 199.09 ms |
| 64 | 250.85 | 735.91 | 18,348.57 ms | 296.42 ms |

The pool explains it: 24,094 tokens against 142,369. At 64 users the BF16 server ran at most 38 requests at a token usage of 0.99 with 26 in the queue; the FP8 server ran all 64 at 0.29 with an empty queue. Goodput at the target was 0 for BF16 at 32 and 64 users and 2.87 requests per second for FP8 at 64. The accuracy check on 500 GSM8K questions gave overlapping intervals for every FP8 configuration, with a KV scale of 1.0 because this model has no scales; run the same check on your own prompts, and read the scale warning in the startup log.

### The shared prompt and the sessions that return

Put the shared system prompt first and keep it byte-identical, with the tool list in a fixed order and nothing that changes per request before the user turn. The pool must then hold the working set. On the L4 with a 2,048-token prompt per group of users, the 24,094-token BF16 pool held about 11 such prompts: at 4 groups the median first token was 360 ms, at 16 groups the GPU-only server evicted prompts it needed again and the first token rose to 3,259 ms, and at 32 groups to 5,449 ms. A host tier held the evicted prompts and gave 553 ms at 16 groups and 817 at 32; at 64 groups the prompts needed more than the GPU and host pools together and the host tier only cut the wait to 3,610 ms from 6,821. With FP8 the pool holds far more prompts, so the first fix for the working set is the pool, and the host tier comes after.

Multi-turn sessions add the same problem over time. In an 8,192-token pool a trace of 24 sessions made the default eviction thrash: the hit rate fell to about 1.5 percent at turns 5 and 6, and a different policy only lifted it to 25 to 34 percent there. A 16,384-token pool reached 0.69 over the whole trace with every policy. Grow the pool before you change the policy, and route each session to the same replica so that its prefix is where it returns.

### Caps

Enforce the knee in the gateway, not only in the engine. The engine admits until memory runs out, and a cap on the engine only chooses who waits: at 32 users on the L4 a cap of 16 moved the median first token from 1.8 to 12.3 s and cut output by 38 percent. Set the gateway limit one or two steps below the measured knee, and shed or queue above it. A second guard on the engine at the same count does no harm.

### Before launch

1. Sweep concurrency with a flush and a new seed before every run, and record the cached tokens. The unflushed sweep put the knee between 16 and 32 users; the flushed one put it between 8 and 16.
2. Record the SM clock and the temperature of every run, cool the card between runs, and set aside runs under a clock floor. Under an open-loop overload the L4 fell from 1,320 to 465 MHz with 70 percent of samples in thermal slowdown, so overload costs throughput as well as latency.
3. Run your real length mix. Fixed lengths form waves and gave a median time to first token of 1,996 ms with a P99 ITL of 82 ms at 16 users; mixed lengths gave 291 ms and 300 ms. The two shapes measure two different servers.
4. Run a fixed arrival rate as well as the closed loop, because real users do not wait for each other.
5. Choose the limit from goodput at the target, and read the P99 ITL next to the first token.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why not take the user count from the throughput peak of the sweep? Expected: throughput peaked at 32 users while no request met the target there, and the knee with a reset was between 8 and 16 users; goodput at the target sets the limit and throughput only explains it.
- **Level 4:** The product adds long sessions that return after minutes. What changes? Expected: the working set grows past the GPU pool, the default eviction drops each session just before it returns, and the hit rate collapses, about 1.5 percent at later turns in an 8,192-token pool; grow the pool first, route each session to the same replica, and add a host tier only when the working set is larger than the GPU pool and smaller than the GPU and host pools together.
- **Level 4:** Traffic doubles for an hour. What protects the users? Expected: a limit at the gateway that sheds or queues above the knee, because the engine admits until memory runs out and a cap on the engine only moves the wait to the first token, and because a passively cooled L4 under overload also loses clock, from 1,320 to 465 MHz, so overload costs throughput as well as latency.
questions.wrong:
- "Run 32 users per card; the sweep showed 275 tokens per second there." No request met the target at 32 users, where the P99 ITL was 613 ms; the knee with a cache reset was between 8 and 16 users.
- "Keep BF16, FP8 is a quality risk we cannot take." On 500 GSM8K questions every FP8 interval overlapped BF16, and FP8 was the difference between zero and 2.87 requests per second within target at 64 users; run the check on your prompts and decide on evidence.
- "Set the engine cap at the knee and you are done." The engine cap only chooses who waits and moved the first token to 12.3 s at 32 users; enforce the knee in the gateway and shed load above it.
- "Benchmark with fixed 512-token prompts, that is the standard." Fixed lengths form waves and gave a first token of 1,996 ms with a P99 ITL of 82 ms, while mixed lengths gave 291 and 300 ms; test your real length mix before you set the limit.

questions.title: Pick the EAGLE3 draft depth for your concurrency
questions.prompt: You turn on an EAGLE3 draft for Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 and must set `num_speculative_tokens`. The draft config suggests a value, but you want to set it yourself. How do you choose, and how does the right value move with the number of users?
questions.short: Set the depth yourself and sweep it at your real concurrency, because the depth that pays falls as more users share each step. On our clock-locked L4 at 32 users, depth 3 gave 333.6 output tokens per second against 208.8 with no speculation, and depth 5 fell back to 289.5, so the extra guesses cost more than they returned. At one user depths 3 and 5 tied, so start at 3 and move only on a measurement.
questions.full:
### Why the depth matters

A deeper draft can give more tokens for each pass of the target, but each guess also costs work in the check. With one user the GPU has spare compute in each step, so extra guesses are almost free. With many users each step is already full, and wrong guesses take compute from real tokens.

### The sweep

Depths 1, 3 and 5 against no speculation, with the clock locked at 900 MHz, 512 tokens in and 128 out, two seeds each:

| Users | Config | Median TPOT | Output tok/s | Median SM clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | no speculation | 119.9 ms | 208.8 | 881 MHz |
| 32 | depth 1 | 100.4 ms | 271.1 | 900 MHz |
| 32 | depth 3 | 77.8 ms | 333.6 | 900 MHz |
| 32 | depth 5 | 83.7 ms | 289.5 | 885 MHz |
| 1 | depth 1 | 39.4 ms | 22.4 | 900 MHz |
| 1 | depth 3 | 27.8 ms | 31.3 | 900 MHz |
| 1 | depth 5 | 26.2 ms | 31.7 | 900 MHz |

At 32 users depth 3 gave 1.6 times the output of no speculation, and its seed range did not overlap with any other config. At one user depth 3 cut the time per token from 39.4 to 27.8 ms against depth 1, and depth 5 was the same within the seeds. The run with no speculation at one user fell to 210 MHz, below the lock, so the manual does not compare it.

### The stream gets lumpier

The median TPOT fell, but the gaps between token groups grew. At 32 users the median ITL rose from 84 ms with no speculation to 133 ms at depth 3. Each step now sends several tokens at once, so the stream arrives in larger and less frequent groups.

### The limits of the result

The gain holds for random prompts and outputs of 128 tokens. Other teams found that synthetic prompts overstate the gain on real prompts and that the best depth changes with the batch size. One study saw the acceptance length fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5 on answers that ran toward 20,000 tokens. The manual's own test up to 4,096 tokens did not see a steady fall; the acceptance stayed near 2.1 to 2.8 tokens per step. So test on your own long answers before you trust the gain.

### Lock the clock before you compare

The first EAGLE3 runs had no lock. At one user the run with no speculation ran at 210 MHz and the EAGLE3 run at about 1,400 MHz. A gap that large hides the effect of speculation, so those runs were set aside. Lock the SM clock with the driver tool before a comparison and release it after, and compare two runs only at the same clock.

### Choose

- Start at 3 for Qwen3-8B with this draft. It gave the best output at 32 users and tied at one.
- For a busy server, sweep the depth on your own model; depth 5 lost output at 32 users here.
- If the load changes a lot through the day, vLLM can set the depth by batch size with `num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size`. The manual did not test it.
- Read the two counters, `spec_decode_num_draft_tokens` and `spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens`, and divide; read the P99 ITL and the P99 TTFT, not only the median.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why did depth 5 lose to depth 3 at 32 users but tie at one user? Expected: at one user the step has spare compute, so two more guesses are nearly free; at 32 users the step is full, and each rejected guess takes compute from real tokens.
- **Level 3:** The median time per token fell and users still said the stream felt uneven. Why? Expected: each step now sends several tokens at once, so tokens arrive in larger and less frequent groups; the median ITL rose from 84 to 133 ms at depth 3 with 32 users.
- **Level 4:** Your load swings from 2 users at night to 32 by day. What do you set? Expected: sweep the depth at both loads, because the depth that pays falls with the batch; vLLM can set the depth per batch size, which the manual did not test, so measure before you trust it.
questions.wrong:
- "Deeper is better, because more guesses mean more tokens per step." At 32 users depth 5 gave 289.5 tokens per second against 333.6 at depth 3; the extra guesses cost more compute than they returned.
- "Leave the depth out and let the draft config decide." Then you do not know what runs; set it yourself so that the number in the command is the number you measured.
- "Compare speculation with the baseline at one user and ship the ratio." The one-user baseline ran at 210 MHz while the EAGLE3 run ran near 1,400 MHz, so the ratio measured the clock; compare at the same clock and at the concurrency you serve.
- "The gain on the random dataset transfers to chat." Synthetic prompts overstate the gain and the acceptance can fall on long answers; measure the acceptance on your own traffic with real output lengths and without ignore-eos.

questions.title: The knee that the prefix cache hid
questions.prompt: Your first concurrency sweep on an L4 shows a first-token median of 0.3 s up to 16 users and 1.8 s at 32, so you set the production limit at 20 users per replica. A second sweep with a reset before each run puts the first token at 1.6 s already at 16 users. Which sweep do you trust, and why do the two disagree?
questions.short: Trust the sweep with the reset. The first sweep kept one server for all the user counts and sent the same first prompts at every count with a fixed seed, so below 32 users many requests found their prompt in the prefix cache and skipped the prefill. With the reset the median first token rose at every step, about 0.65 s at 4 users, 1.0 s at 8 and 1.6 s at 16, and the P99 ITL jumped from about 70 ms at 8 users to 522 ms at 16, so the knee on this card sits between 8 and 16 users, not between 16 and 32.
questions.full:
### How the cache inflated the first sweep

The random dataset with a fixed seed sends the same prompts in every run. The first sweep ran all the user counts against one server, so each run found the prompts of the earlier runs in the cache. This was the table it produced, Qwen/Qwen3-8B on vLLM 0.31.0, three seeds per point:

| Users | Output tok/s | Median TTFT | Median TPOT | P99 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 13.5 | 191 ms | 60.4 ms | 105 ms |
| 8 | 112.8 | 253 ms | 65.8 ms | 67 ms |
| 16 | 201.3 | 288 ms | 69.5 ms | 85 ms |
| 32 | 275.1 | 1,800 ms | 101.8 ms | 613 ms |
| 64 | 242.3 | 11,181 ms | 129.2 ms | 1,233 ms |

The jump between 16 and 32 users looked like the knee. It was the throughput peak. A cached prompt skips its prefill, so its first token comes fast, and most requests below 32 users had that advantage.

### The flushed comparison

The same sweep at 900 MHz, the cache reset ahead of every run, against an unflushed run of the same session:

| Users | vLLM, flushed against unflushed | SGLang, flushed against unflushed |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 650 / 145 ms | 532 to 645 / 141 ms |
| 8 | 951 to 978 / 264 to 274 ms | 1,174 to 1,273 / 173 to 178 ms |
| 16 | 1,550 to 1,587 / 294 to 295 ms | 1,804 to 1,944 / 218 ms |
| 32 | 1,982 to 2,084 / 2,012 to 3,091 ms | 3,216 to 3,228 / 2,710 to 2,917 ms |

From 32 users the queue dominated and the reset changed little. Below it, the cache made most of the fast first tokens.

### The size of the effect on one load

The same 64 prompts at 16 users, four times in a row, median TTFT in ms: vLLM read 925 fresh, 148 on a repeat without a flush, 1,163 on a repeat after a flush, and 184 on another repeat without one. SGLang read 394, 82.5, 289 and 77. The repeat without a flush read a first token about 6 times lower on vLLM and 4.8 times lower on SGLang. The time per token changed by less than 15 percent, because a hit removes prefill work and leaves the decode work the same.

On the GB10 the effect reversed a sweep. A single kit run read 677.61 ms as the median time to first token with a cap of 8 and 390.38 ms with a cap of 32: more load, a faster first token. The prefill lines showed why. At a cap of 8, 16 of the 64 prompts were in the cache before the run started; at 32, 64 of 128; at 64, 128 of 256. Three seeds with fresh servers put the first token back in order, 209.98 ms at 8 and 416.37 at 32.

### The protocol

1. Start each run with an empty cache. Restart the server, or call the reset route: `POST /reset_prefix_cache` on vLLM, which exists only with `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1` and must never be exposed, or `--flush-cache` on the SGLang client, which calls `/flush_cache` after the warm-up. SGLang flushes only when no request runs or waits; otherwise the route answers HTTP 400 and the log says so.
2. Use a new seed for each run, so that the random dataset sends new prompts.
3. Record the cached tokens. Read the prefix cache counters before and after the run, or turn on the per-response count, `--enable-prompt-tokens-details` on vLLM and `--enable-cache-report` on SGLang.
4. Write the cache setting and the cached tokens next to the result.

The vLLM sweep tool resets the server caches between its runs for you.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why did the time per token barely move between the flushed and the unflushed runs? Expected: a cache hit removes prefill work and leaves the decode work the same, so TTFT falls and TPOT moves by less than 15 percent.
- **Level 3:** On the GB10 a single run read a faster first token at a cap of 32 than at a cap of 8. How is that possible? Expected: the runs shared one server and one seed, so the run at 32 found 64 of its 128 prompts in the cache from the earlier runs and half of its requests skipped prefill; three seeds on fresh servers put the first token back in order.
- **Level 3:** The flush route on SGLang answered HTTP 400. What happened? Expected: the server flushes only when no request runs or waits; a request was still pending, so the flush did not run and the log says so, and the run must wait or restart the server.
- **Level 4:** How would you make the warm-cache effect part of a benchmark on purpose? Expected: measure it as its own axis; record the cached tokens per run from the counters or the per-response field, and report a warm-cache row next to a cold row, each with its hit rate, instead of letting an unknown mix of the two set the knee.
questions.wrong:
- "The jump from 0.3 to 1.8 s between 16 and 32 users is the knee." That sweep ran without a reset, so most requests below 32 users skipped their prefill; with a reset the P99 ITL jumped from about 70 to 522 ms between 8 and 16 users, and that is the knee.
- "Turn the prefix cache off for benchmarks." Production runs with it on; reset it between runs, use a new seed per run and record the cached tokens instead.
- "The time per token is inflated too, so throw the whole sweep away." A hit removes prefill work only; the time per token changed by less than 15 percent between flushed and unflushed runs, so the TPOT column stands and the TTFT column does not.
- "The random dataset gives new prompts every run." With the same seed the client sends the same prompts; the dataset is random only across seeds, so use a new seed per run.

questions.title: What an FP8 KV cache buys and costs
questions.prompt: Your server queues requests because the KV cache is full. Someone suggests `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`. What does it buy, what can it cost, and how do you check both before production?
questions.short: An FP8 KV cache stores each key and value in 1 byte instead of 2, so the same memory holds twice the tokens: for Qwen/Qwen3-8B a token falls from 144 KiB to 72 KiB, and one GiB holds about 14,600 tokens instead of about 7,300. It can cost accuracy, because FP8 needs a scale per tensor and a checkpoint without scales runs with a scale of 1.0, and it can change the attention backend, which on our L4 broke the first start. Check it with an accuracy run on your own task and with the startup log: on 500 GSM8K questions our FP8 KV run scored 90.8 percent against 91.8 in BF16, with overlapping intervals.
questions.full:
### What it buys

Only the cache changes; the weights stay in BF16. Use the KV formula with 1 byte per value. Twice the tokens fit, so twice the users fit at the same length, or each user can have a context twice as long.

The speed change is small. With the pool held fixed at 24,096 tokens on our L4, one user got a median TPOT of 101.8 ms against 104.1 ms in BF16, 2.3 percent faster at the same 210 MHz clock, and the seed ranges did not overlap. At 32 users the seed ranges overlapped and the FP8 run had a higher clock, so the manual claims no gain there. Two things changed together in that run, the cache dtype and the attention backend.

A field report shows the capacity effect at scale. With a BF16 cache a service produced 1,558 tokens per second at 32 concurrent requests and ran out of memory at 64. With an FP8 cache it reached 2,192 tokens per second at 64, about 41 percent above the best BF16 result, while it was a few percent slower per token at every concurrency both could run. It won because twice as many requests fit: the context held in memory went from about 686,000 to about 1.37 million tokens.

### What it costs

FP8 needs a scale for each tensor. Without a scale file, every scale is 1.0. vLLM logs `Using KV cache scaling factor 1.0` and SGLang logs `Using FP8 KV cache but no scaling factors provided`. The vLLM team treats a scale of 1.0 as the worst case for accuracy; in their tests most models stayed close to BF16, and one model family on a latent-attention backend did not.

Our own check, on 2026-10-23, ran the first 500 GSM8K questions, 8-shot and greedy, on the L4. Qwen3-8B has no KV scales, so the FP8 KV runs used a scale of 1.0:

| Engine | Config | Correct | Accuracy | Wilson 95 percent interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vLLM | BF16 | 459/500 | 91.8% | 89.1 to 93.9 |
| vLLM | FP8 KV cache | 454/500 | 90.8% | 87.9 to 93.0 |
| SGLang | BF16 | 458/500 | 91.6% | 88.8 to 93.7 |
| SGLang | FP8 KV cache | 458/500 | 91.6% | 88.8 to 93.7 |

Every interval overlaps the BF16 interval, so this run did not show a difference. With 500 questions it cannot rule out a loss of a few points. It is one model and one benchmark. A model with a different attention layout can lose more.

### The backend trap on an L4

The first FP8 start on our L4 failed. FlashAttention in vLLM 0.31.0 reads an FP8 cache only on Hopper and Blackwell data center GPUs, and the L4 is an Ada GPU, SM 8.9. So vLLM moved to FlashInfer, which builds its kernels on the first start, and that build failed on our node. The fix was `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`, which reads FP8 and needs no build, with `VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0` for the same reason. Read the attention backend line after every change to the cache dtype.

### Check that your scales load

1. Search the weight index of the checkpoint for tensor names that end in `k_scale` or `v_scale`. For a checkpoint with an index, no output means no scales. A checkpoint with one weight file has no index; for it, list the tensor names with the `safetensors` Python package.
2. Read the startup log for the scale warning. If the checkpoint has scales and the warning still prints, the loader dropped them. At 0.31.0 one model family never loads its KV scales, and the issue is open.
3. Run your own prompts with and without FP8 and compare the answers before you go to production.

The FP8 checkpoint of Qwen3-30B-A3B lists weight scales and no KV scales, so weight scales do not imply KV scales.

### The order of checks

1. Is the pool the limit? Read the cache usage and the queue. If the pool has room, keep the model dtype.
2. Search the checkpoint for KV scales.
3. Start the server and read the backend line and the scale warning.
4. Run an accuracy check on your own task.
5. Measure speed at the same clock, and expect little change per token.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** The pool has room and requests do not queue. Do you still switch? Expected: no; the cache dtype is a capacity decision, and with room in the pool it buys nothing and still carries the accuracy and backend risks.
- **Level 3:** The scale warning prints although the checkpoint has k_scale tensors. What does it mean? Expected: the loader dropped the scales; at 0.31.0 one model family never loads its KV scales and the issue is open, so the server runs with a scale of 1.0 until you change the checkpoint or the version.
- **Level 3:** Why did the first FP8 start fail on the L4 and not on a data center GPU? Expected: the default attention backend reads an FP8 cache only on Hopper and Blackwell data center GPUs, so vLLM fell back to a backend that compiles its kernels on the first start, and that build failed; the Triton backend reads FP8 and skips the build.
- **Level 4:** The GSM8K check gave 91.8 against 90.8 percent, and the two intervals overlap. What can you conclude? Expected: this run did not show a difference and cannot rule out a loss of a few points; it is one model and one benchmark, so run the same check on your model and task, and expect a model with another attention layout to lose more.
questions.wrong:
- "FP8 KV halves memory, so it doubles throughput." It doubles the tokens that fit; in the field report it was a few percent slower per token at every load both caches could run, and won only because the BF16 cache ran out at 64 requests.
- "The checkpoint is FP8, so the KV scales are there." Weight scales and KV scales are different tensors; the FP8 checkpoint of Qwen3-30B-A3B lists weight scales and no k_scale or v_scale, so its cache ran with a scale of 1.0.
- "Accuracy is a property of the model, so test it once." The loss depends on the model, the attention layout and the task; one family that needs calibrated scales lost accuracy with a scale of 1.0 while most models stayed close to BF16 in the same tests.
- "The attention backend does not matter for a cache dtype." On the L4 the dtype change moved vLLM to another backend and the start failed; read the backend line after every change to the cache dtype.

questions.title: When an FP8 checkpoint pays
questions.prompt: Your Qwen/Qwen3-8B server in BF16 fits on one L4, but only with a small KV pool. The model's publisher also offers an FP8 checkpoint. When does the FP8 checkpoint pay, what does it do to speed, and what does our GSM8K check say about the cost?
questions.short: FP8 weights store most parameters in 1 byte instead of 2, so they free memory that the engine gives to the KV pool, and on a GPU with FP8 math they also speed up the matrix work. On our clock-locked L4 with the pool held fixed, the FP8 checkpoint gave 284.7 against 208.8 output tokens per second at 32 users, 36 percent more, and cut the time per token by 30 percent. On 500 GSM8K questions it scored 90.6 percent against 91.8 in BF16, 1.2 points lower with overlapping intervals, so the run did not show a loss and cannot rule out a few points.
questions.full:
### Serve it

Serve the published checkpoint like any model, `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8`, and set no flag. vLLM reads the quantization method from the checkpoint config. SGLang does the same, and a `--quantization` flag that does not match the checkpoint raises at startup, except for a few known compatible pairs. If no FP8 checkpoint exists, vLLM can quantize a BF16 model when it loads; the manual did not test that path.

### Know what your GPU runs

The L4 is an Ada GPU, SM 8.9, and it has FP8 math, so the matrix math runs in FP8 and the speed can rise with the free memory. GPUs before Ada, such as the A100, have no FP8 math. There vLLM keeps the weights in FP8 and runs a weight-only kernel: you keep the memory saving and expect less speed gain. The manual did not test such a GPU.

### The L4 result

The session locked at 900 MHz, two seeds each, the pool held at 24,096 tokens in both runs:

| Users | Median TPOT, BF16 / FP8 | Output tok/s, BF16 / FP8 | Median SM clock, BF16 / FP8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | 119.9 / 83.8 ms | 208.8 / 284.7 | 881 / 900 MHz |
| 1 | not compared / 35.3 ms | not compared / 25.4 | 210 / 900 MHz |

At 32 users the seed ranges did not overlap for either number, and the BF16 clock was about 2 percent lower, much less than the gap. At one user the BF16 run fell to 210 MHz because the GPU throttled, so the two are not compared.

### What it frees

The speed test held the pool fixed, so it did not measure the larger pool. The gain in room comes from the bytes. The SGLang runs on the same L4 let the pool grow and changed the weights and the cache together: the pool went from 24,094 tokens in BF16 to 142,369 with FP8 weights and an FP8 cache, 5.91 times as many, and output at 64 users went from 250.85 to 735.91 tokens per second, because the BF16 pool was full and the FP8 pool was not. At one user FP8 was still faster, 39.66 against 60.16 ms per token, because decode reads every weight for every token and FP8 weights are half the bytes.

On the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B the FP8 pair did the same: the weights went from 57.75 to 29.75 GB, the load time from 323.61 to 152.29 s, and the pool from 227,243 to 1,083,008 tokens, 4.77 times as many, because the smaller weights freed memory and each token took half the bytes. Throughput was 1.73 to 1.88 times higher at every concurrency, because decode on that machine reads weights from a memory with modest bandwidth.

### The accuracy check

The first 500 GSM8K questions, 8-shot and greedy, on the L4 on 2026-10-23:

| Engine | Config | Correct | Accuracy | Wilson 95 percent interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vLLM | BF16 | 459/500 | 91.8% | 89.1 to 93.9 |
| vLLM | FP8 weights | 453/500 | 90.6% | 87.7 to 92.9 |
| vLLM | FP8 weights + FP8 KV | 453/500 | 90.6% | 87.7 to 92.9 |
| SGLang | BF16 | 458/500 | 91.6% | 88.8 to 93.7 |
| SGLang | FP8 weights | 456/500 | 91.2% | 88.4 to 93.4 |
| SGLang | FP8 weights + FP8 KV | 460/500 | 92.0% | 89.3 to 94.1 |

All intervals overlap. The run did not show a difference, and with 500 questions it cannot rule out a loss of a few points. It is one model and one benchmark. Run your own prompts on both checkpoints before production.

### When it does not pay

- The pool has room and the GPU has no FP8 math: little gain for the risk.
- A task that depends on long chains of reasoning: run your own check first.
- The model still does not fit in FP8: a 4-bit checkpoint stores most weights in about half a byte, and on a 24 GB card that is the common way to serve a 14B model. A 4-bit model can lose more accuracy than FP8, and the loss depends on the model and the method.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** The pool was held fixed in the speed test. What did that hide, and what did it show? Expected: it hid the larger pool that FP8 frees, so the test shows only the change in speed; the gain in room comes from the bytes, and the SGLang run that let the pool grow went from 24,094 to 142,369 tokens with an FP8 cache too.
- **Level 3:** Why was the one-user row not compared? Expected: the BF16 run fell to 210 MHz, below the 900 MHz lock, because the GPU throttled; a lock caps the clock and cannot stop a throttle, so the two runs were at different clocks.
- **Level 4:** On the GB10 the FP8 pair nearly doubled the speed at every load, while a field report of an FP8 cache alone was a little slower per token. Reconcile the two. Expected: the GB10 decodes from a memory with modest bandwidth, so half the weight bytes gave almost twice the speed; an FP8 cache alone changes no weight bytes and adds the scale work, so it wins on capacity and not on speed per token.
questions.wrong:
- "FP8 always speeds up decode." Only on a GPU with FP8 math, such as Ada, Hopper and Blackwell; on an A100 vLLM keeps the weights in FP8 and runs a weight-only kernel, so you keep the memory saving and expect less speed gain.
- "Pass --quantization fp8 to be safe." vLLM reads the method from the checkpoint config, and in SGLang a flag that does not match the checkpoint raises at startup, so pass no flag for a published checkpoint.
- "A 1.2 point drop on GSM8K means FP8 loses accuracy." The two intervals overlap, so this run did not show a difference; it also cannot rule out a loss of a few points, which is why you run your own prompts on both checkpoints.
- "If FP8 is good, 4-bit is twice as good." A 4-bit model can lose more accuracy than an FP8 model, and the loss depends on the model and the method; use it when the model does not fit in FP8, such as a 14B model on a 24 GB card, and test it.

questions.title: Why 255 tokens per second is a slogan
questions.prompt: A teammate posts in the team channel that the server does 255 tokens per second. Is that a result? What would you ask for, and what single number tells you where to stop adding users?
questions.short: It is a slogan, not a result, because a throughput number without the latency that came with it describes nothing a user feels. Ask for the concurrency, the median and P99 first token and time per token at that concurrency, the client and the temperature, and the clock. Goodput is the number that sets the limit: the requests per second, or the share of requests, that met every latency target at once, and on the manual's GB10 the BF16 server's goodput was highest at a cap of 4 while its throughput kept rising to a cap of 64.
questions.full:
### The same server, two loads

The 255 came from the manual's own capture. The same server gave that throughput with a median time to first token of 0.8 s at one load and 3.9 s at another:

| Cap | Output tok/s | Median TTFT | P99 TTFT | Median TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 175.15 | 162.98 ms | 270.18 ms | 4.38 ms |
| 8 | 255.63 | 785.79 ms | 2180.87 ms | 22.52 ms |
| 32 | 252.74 | 3917.54 ms | 8262.86 ms | 93.61 ms |

From a cap of 8 to 32 the throughput fell about 1 percent, the median first token got 5 times slower, and the median time per token got 4.2 times slower. The server had no idle compute left to give; new users only waited for a share of the same steps.

### Goodput

Goodput is the share of requests, or the rate of requests per second, that met every latency bound at the same time: the first token under a limit, the time per token under a limit, and the end-to-end time under a limit. A request that misses any one of them is not good. The lesson's rule: high throughput at 60 percent goodput is failure, and lower throughput at 99 percent goodput is the target.

The manual's target was a first token under 1 s and a mean time per token under 100 ms. On the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B:

| Cap | BF16 goodput | BF16 median TPOT | FP8 goodput | FP8 median TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.44 req/s | 71.01 ms | 0.80 req/s | 38.60 ms |
| 8 | 0, up to 0.04 in one seed | 102.21 ms | 1.07 req/s | 54.96 ms |
| 16 | 0 | 154.24 ms | 1.10 req/s | 81.90 ms |
| 32 | 0 | 201.91 ms | 0 | 104.12 ms |

BF16 goodput was highest at a cap of 4. At a cap of 8 the median request took longer than 100 ms per token, so at least half of the requests missed the target, and goodput was 0, up to 0.04 in one seed, while throughput at that cap was 74.11 tokens per second and still rising. FP8 held the target up to a cap of 16. Choose the cap from goodput at your own target, and use the throughput curve only to explain it.

### Why the mean is the wrong statistic

The lesson gives the shape: a decode batch with one long prefill neighbour can ship most tokens near 7 ms per token and a few near 60 ms, so the mean reads 9 ms while the P99 reads 65 ms, and users hit the P99 regularly. Report the median, the P90 and the P99 together. The tools also disagree on the definition: for a request with a 500 ms first token and 100 output tokens over 700 ms of decode, one tool that excludes the first token reports 7.07 ms per token and one that includes it reports 12.00 ms. State the tool and the definition with every number.

### Where the knee is, and who enforces it

A closed loop never falls behind, because each client waits for its answer before it sends the next request. A fixed arrival rate does not wait. Under a fixed rate the GB10 BF16 server already had a median time per token of 177.5 ms at 0.5 requests per second and met the target for only 0.07 requests per second, while FP8 met the target for every request up to 1 per second and fell to 0.17 at 2. Enforce the knee outside the engine, in the client or the gateway, because the engine's own admission limit comes from memory and sat at 4096 running requests on that server, far above the knee.

### The floor behind one number

The lesson shows where the time per token comes from on an L4: one decode step reads 16.41 GB of weights, which takes at least 54.7 ms at 300 GB/s, and the measured step took 60.16 ms. A target of 100 ms per token leaves little room on that card for an 8B model in BF16, which is why the pool and the precision matter before the scheduler does.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Which numbers go next to a throughput figure? Expected: the concurrency or request rate, and the median and P99 of the first token and of the time per token at that point, with the client, temperature and clock as context.
- **Level 2:** Goodput fell to zero at a cap of 8 while throughput still rose. How can both be true? Expected: the server wrote more tokens per second, but the median request took longer than 100 ms per token, so at least half of the requests missed the target and almost none met every bound; throughput counts tokens and goodput counts requests that arrived on time.
- **Level 3:** Why is the mean the wrong statistic for the time per token? Expected: the distribution has a long right tail; a batch with one long prefill neighbour can ship most tokens near 7 ms and a few near 60, so the mean reads 9 ms while the P99 reads 65, and users hit the P99 regularly.
- **Level 4:** Two tools report different time per token for the same run. Why, and what do you do? Expected: one excludes the first token from the inter-token calculation and the other includes it, 7.07 against 12.00 ms in the lesson's example; state the tool and the definition with every number, and keep one tool for every run you compare.
questions.wrong:
- "255 tokens per second is the capacity of the server." The same server gave that throughput with a median time to first token of 0.8 s at one load and 3.9 s at another; the number without its latency is not a result.
- "Add users until throughput stops rising, then stop." On the GB10 the BF16 throughput kept rising to a cap of 64 while goodput was 0 or close to it from a cap of 8; the latency target, not the throughput curve, sets the limit.
- "Report the mean time per token." The distribution is right-skewed, so a mean of 9 ms can hide a P99 of 65; report the median, P90 and P99.
- "The engine's own admission limit protects the users." The engine's limit comes from memory, which runs out long after latency is unacceptable; enforce the knee in the client or the gateway.

questions.title: Pick a concurrency cap when throughput keeps rising
questions.prompt: You serve a chat model on one GPU. A load sweep shows output throughput that still rises at a cap of 64 concurrent requests, so the team wants to set the cap to 64. The product needs the first token in under one second and a steady stream of text after it. Which cap do you pick, and how do you defend it?
questions.short: Pick the cap from goodput, not from throughput. Goodput counts only the requests that meet every latency target, so it falls to zero long before throughput stops rising. On the sweep in the SGLang manual, BF16 goodput was highest at a cap of 4 and was 0 from a cap of 8. Use the throughput curve only to explain the choice.
questions.full:
### Why throughput hides the knee

A large KV pool lets the server admit more requests. On the GB10 in the manual, the pool held 234,600 tokens, so BF16 throughput still rose at a cap of 64. More admitted requests share each decode step, so each request gets fewer tokens per second. Throughput measures the server. Latency measures the user.

### Define the target first

The manual counts a request as good when its first token comes in under 1 s and its mean time per token is under 100 ms. Write the target down before the sweep. A goodput number without its target means nothing.

### Read the sweep

| Cap | BF16 goodput | BF16 median TPOT | FP8 goodput | FP8 median TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.44 req/s | 71.01 ms | 0.80 req/s | 38.60 ms |
| 8 | 0 | 102.21 ms | 1.07 req/s | 54.96 ms |
| 16 | 0 | 154.24 ms | 1.10 req/s | 81.90 ms |
| 32 | 0 | 201.91 ms | 0 | 104.12 ms |

At a cap of 8, the median BF16 request already takes more than 100 ms per token. Throughput at that cap is 74.11 tok/s and still rising. FP8 holds the target up to a cap of 16. So the answer depends on the build: about 4 for BF16 and about 16 for FP8 on this machine.

### Defend it

- Run three seeds per point and show the band, so that a reviewer can see the gaps are real.
- Reset the prefix cache before each run. A warm cache makes the first token look fast.
- A cap is a closed loop. Real users arrive on their own clock, so also run an open-loop sweep with a request rate and check goodput there.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What is the difference between throughput and goodput? Expected: throughput counts all tokens or requests per second; goodput counts only the requests that met every latency target.
- **Level 3:** Why can a closed-loop cap never show a growing queue? Expected: each client waits for its answer before it sends the next request, so the server never receives more work than it finishes.
- **Level 3:** FP8 holds the target at a cap of 16 and BF16 does not. What do you check before you switch the build? Expected: output quality on your own eval, and the KV pool size, because FP8 frees memory for a larger pool.
- **Level 4:** The GPU gets hot at high load. How does that change your sweep? Expected: record the GPU clock and the thermal state with every run, and let the GPU cool to a fixed temperature before each run.
questions.wrong:
- "Set the cap where throughput peaks." The throughput curve had no peak inside the sweep, and every BF16 request missed the target from a cap of 8.
- "Use the median TTFT alone." A median can hide a slow half of the requests, and the time per token can fail while the first token is fast.
- "Report goodput from one run." One run can be wrong for reasons you never see, so use three seeds and report the range.

questions.title: How speculative decoding keeps the output the same
questions.prompt: Speculative decoding promises several tokens per step with no change to what the model writes. Explain how the engine keeps that promise, where the speedup comes from, and why the gain shrinks as more users share the server.
questions.short: A cheap proposer guesses the next few tokens, and the target model runs once over all the guesses and computes its own distribution at every position. A rejection sampler keeps each guess that the target supports, samples a correct token from the target at the first rejection, and stops, so one pass gives at least one token and at most the number of guesses plus one, with the same output distribution as plain decoding. The gain comes from idle GPU time: a small decode batch waits for memory, and as the batch grows that idle time goes away, so the checks of rejected guesses start to cost real compute.
questions.full:
### Guess, then check

A decode step on a small batch reads all the weights to produce one token per request, and most of the GPU sits idle while it waits for memory. Speculation uses that idle time. With greedy sampling a guess stays only if it equals the top token of the target at that position. With random sampling the rejection rule keeps the output distribution equal to the target's distribution. In SGLang the accept thresholds default to 1.0, so a greedy request produces the same tokens it would produce without speculation.

The acceptance length is the number of tokens committed per verify pass: the accepted drafts plus one bonus token from the target. One real Qwen3-8B request on our L4 got about 1.8 tokens per pass.

### The proposers

| Method | Where the guesses come from |
|---|---|
| `ngram` | earlier text in the same request that matches the last few tokens |
| `suffix` | a suffix tree over earlier prompts and answers |
| `eagle`, `eagle3` | a small draft head that reads the hidden states of the target |
| `*_mtp` | extra prediction heads that come with some models |
| `draft_model` | a separate small model |

N-gram costs almost nothing and needs no extra weights. It pays when the answer copies the prompt: an edit of a document, a summary that quotes the source, a code change that keeps most lines, extraction from a long input. On our L4 with random prompts it cut the time per token from 241.7 to 76.6 ms at one user, and at four users the P99 ITL rose from 290 to 1,691 ms. It also turns off async scheduling, with only a warning in the log. An EAGLE3 head needs training for your target; the public head for Qwen3-8B has one layer and a draft vocabulary of 32,000 tokens.

### Why the gain falls with load

The idle time exists only while the step reads more memory than it computes. As the batch grows, the step does more compute for each byte, and the idle time goes away. The checks of rejected guesses then cost real compute. One report shows both ends on the same GPU and model: at batch 1 output went from 42.0 to 92.5 tokens per second, and at concurrency 20 it fell from 217.8 to 164.4. The maintainer's answer was that speculation is meant for small batches. The dynamic mode follows from this rule: it sets the number of guesses from the batch size and stops guessing for large batches.

### The lesson's arithmetic

Expected tokens per target forward are 1 + K x alpha, with K the draft length and alpha the acceptance rate. For K of 5 and alpha of 0.7, with about 10 percent verify overhead, that is 4.5 divided by 1.1, about 4.1 times. Real gains cluster around 2 to 3 times, because alpha is rarely that high on production traffic and the overhead grows with the batch. The lesson puts the break-even alpha at high concurrency near 0.45 to 0.55.

### What to watch

The engine exports the proposed and the accepted tokens. Divide accepted by proposed for the acceptance rate, and read the mean tokens per step. A high acceptance rate with no gain in the time per token means the batch is already compute bound.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Which proposer needs no extra model, and when does it pay? Expected: n-gram, which matches the last tokens of the output against earlier text in the request; it pays for edits, quotes, code changes and extraction, and fails on open chat.
- **Level 3:** Acceptance is high but the time per token did not fall. What does that tell you? Expected: the batch is already compute bound; the idle memory time that speculation uses is gone, so the checks cost as much as they save.
- **Level 3:** With greedy sampling, how does the check decide at each position? Expected: a guess stays only if it equals the top token of the target there; the first mismatch is replaced by the target's token and the rest are dropped.
- **Level 4:** Why can one verify pass never commit more tokens than the draft length plus one? Expected: the target computes a distribution at every draft position and one past the last guess, so when all guesses pass the sampler still draws one bonus token from that last distribution; at a rejection it samples a correct token there and stops.
questions.wrong:
- "Speculation changes the output a little, so you trade some quality for speed." With greedy sampling a guess stays only if it equals the target's top token, and with random sampling the rejection rule keeps the output distribution equal to the target's, so the quality does not change, although one sampled run can differ from a run without speculation.
- "The draft is where the speed comes from, so a faster draft always helps." The gain comes from idle GPU time in a small batch; a fast draft with low acceptance adds checks that cost compute, and at concurrency 20 one report lost a quarter of its throughput.
- "Turn it on for the stress test too." At batch 1 one report more than doubled its speed and at concurrency 20 it was slower; the maintainer's answer was that speculation is for small batches.

questions.title: How many users fit in the KV pool
questions.prompt: You serve `Qwen/Qwen3-8B` on one GPU with a maximum model length of 8,192 tokens. At startup the server prints a maximum concurrency of 2.94, and a manager asks if the GPU can serve only three users at a time. Your users send about 512 prompt tokens and get about 128 tokens back. How do you answer?
questions.short: The startup number assumes that every user fills the full maximum model length, and real users hold much less. Count the KV bytes for one token, divide the KV pool by that number, and then divide the pool by the context that one user really holds. On the L4 in the vLLM manual, the pool of 24,096 tokens fits 37 users with 640 tokens each.
questions.full:
### Bytes for one token

Every token in a running request keeps its keys and values in GPU memory until the request ends:

```text
KV bytes per token = layers x KV heads x head size x 2 x bytes per value
```

The factor 2 counts the key and the value. `Qwen/Qwen3-8B` has 36 layers, 8 KV heads and a head size of 128. In BF16 a value takes 2 bytes, so one token takes 144 KiB. The KV heads decide this number, not the parameter count: `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507` has more weights but takes 96 KiB for each token.

### From bytes to users

The server gives the KV cache the memory that is left after the weights and the startup profile. The pool line in the log gives the result in tokens:

```text
GPU KV cache size: 24,096 tokens, Maximum concurrency for 8,192 tokens per request: 2.94x
```

The 2.94 divides the pool by the full 8,192 tokens. A user with 512 prompt tokens and 128 output tokens holds 640 tokens at the end of the answer. The same pool holds 37 such users. During the load sweep the log showed 40 running requests with the cache 99.5 percent full, because users early in their answer hold fewer tokens.

### What to change if it is still too small

1. Lower the maximum model length to the longest context that users send. This keeps one long request from taking a large share of the pool. It does not add users here, because the pool stays the same.
2. Use an FP8 KV cache. It halves the bytes per token.
3. Use FP8 weights to free memory for the cache.
4. Use a GPU with more memory, or split the model across GPUs.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What happens to a request that needs more blocks than are free? Expected: it waits in the queue. A running request that needs a block when none is free is stopped and computed again later.
- **Level 2:** Why does the mixture-of-experts model use less KV memory per token than the dense model? Expected: it has fewer KV heads, and the KV heads, not the weights, set the bytes per token.
- **Level 3:** How do you check your count after a start? Expected: read the memory line and the pool line in the startup log, and compare them with the count from the model config.
- **Level 3:** What is the cost of the FP8 KV cache? Expected: a possible loss of quality, so measure it on your own eval before you ship it.
questions.wrong:
- "Divide the GPU memory by the model size." The weights are only one part. The users that fit depend on the KV pool and on the context per user.
- "The maximum concurrency in the log is the user limit." It assumes that each user fills the maximum model length, which real users do not.
- "More parameters always mean more KV memory per token." The bytes per token depend on the layers, the KV heads and the head size.

questions.title: Cached tokens at zero with a stable template
questions.prompt: A team runs long agent sessions on SGLang with hierarchical caching on. Their dashboards show `#cached-token: 0` on requests that resend a long history. They have tuned the cache tiers and the write policy, and the hit rate barely moves. The prompt template looks stable to them. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find?
questions.short: Look at the first tokens of the request as the server sees them, not at the template. A relay or a chat template often adds something that changes on every request near the start, such as a request ID, a session hash or the date, and the tree matches from the first token and stops at the first difference. In the manual's incident a random hash in the system prompt cost 27.6 points of hit rate, and removing it moved the engine hit rate from 66.8 to 94.4 percent.
questions.full:
### Reproduce it with one identifier in three places

The manual's capture kit sends one 2,999-token system prompt and a short question, five times in each of three forms, with `--enable-cache-report` on so that each response reports its cached tokens:

| Form | Cached tokens | Prompt tokens | Median TTFT |
|---|---|---|---|
| stable system prompt | 2,998 | 2,999 | 45.1 ms |
| random ID at the start | 5 | 3,034 | 1,255.3 ms |
| the same ID at the end | 2,985 | 3,028 | 88.2 ms |

The ID at the start made the first token 28 times slower. The ID at the end cost 43 ms. The tokens are almost the same in the three forms; only their order differs. The ID at the start matched the 5 tokens before the random hex digits and nothing after them.

### Why nothing after a change can match

The attention values of every later token depend on every earlier token. A cache that reused the later tokens would return wrong answers. So the tree is exact, and a change in the system prompt invalidates everything behind it, while a change in the newest message invalidates only that message.

### The incident behind the question

The reporter found three causes stacked on each other:

1. The relay put a per-session random hash and a rotating system message into every request. Removing them moved the engine hit rate from 66.8 to 94.4 percent.
2. The client wrote its task-list snapshot at the end of the system prompt. Every task update changed the system prompt and invalidated more than 100,000 tokens of history behind it.
3. Hierarchical cache load-back, when it found no room, evicted the prefixes of other sessions. The reporter counted 250,000 evict calls against 376 completed load-backs.

The first fix was a prompt edit. No cache flag could have recovered the 27.6 points that the hash cost. The lesson tells the same story from another deployment, where moving dynamic content out of the cacheable prefix took the hit rate from 7 to 74 percent.

### The order of checks

1. Dump the exact token sequence of two consecutive requests and compare them from the first token. Include what the relay and the chat template add.
2. Read `cached_tokens` in the usage block with `--enable-cache-report`, or in `meta_info` of the native `/generate` route.
3. Read `#new-token` and `#cached-token` in the `Prefill batch` lines.
4. Read `sglang:cache_hit_rate` from `/metrics`.
5. With several servers, check routing. A request that lands on a server without its prefix misses whatever the prompt looks like. One report moved from 64.7 to 92.1 percent by routing each conversation to the same server.

Two server settings look like prompt problems. A request for prompt log probabilities from position k can reuse only the first k tokens. Different LoRA adapters never share tree nodes, because the adapter is part of the tree key.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** The same random ID moves behind the fixed text instead. What does it cost now? Expected: about 45 tokens of prefill instead of about 3,027; in the experiment that was 43 ms more than the stable prompt instead of 28 times longer.
- **Level 3:** After the prompt fix, one server hits well and the fleet still misses. What next? Expected: routing; a request that lands on a server without its prefix misses, and routing each conversation to the same server moved one report from 64.7 to 92.1 percent.
- **Level 4:** The host tier still hurts other sessions after the prompt fix. What did the incident count, and what does it mean? Expected: 250,000 evict calls against 376 completed load-backs; a load-back that finds no room evicts other sessions from the GPU pool, so the pool size and the write policy need a look only after the prompt is fixed.
questions.wrong:
- "Raise the hierarchical cache ratio until the hit rate recovers." No cache flag can recover a miss that starts at token 5; the first fix was a prompt edit, worth 27.6 points of hit rate.
- "The template is stable, so the prompt is stable." The template is not what the server sees; a relay, a gateway or the chat template can insert a hash, a date or a snapshot, so compare the token sequences of two consecutive requests from the start.
- "A changed field in the middle only costs the tokens of that field." Every token after the change is a different branch of the tree, because the attention values of later tokens depend on every earlier token.

questions.title: What many LoRA adapters cost one server
questions.prompt: You have twenty fine-tunes of one base model, each a LoRA adapter, and you want to serve them from one vLLM server. What do you set, what decides the cost, and what else in the server changes when LoRA is on?
questions.short: Turn LoRA on at startup with `--enable-lora`, name the adapters with `--lora-modules`, and let each request pick one in its `model` field. Three limits set the cost: `--max-loras`, which defaults to 1 and caps the adapters that run in one batch, `--max-lora-rank`, which defaults to 16 and reserves memory for the largest rank, and `--max-cpu-loras` for adapters kept in CPU memory ready to load. LoRA also changes the prefix cache, because the adapter is part of every block key, so two adapters never share cached blocks, and it adds CUDA graphs per adapter, so startup takes longer and uses more memory.
questions.full:
### Start it

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --enable-lora \
  --lora-modules support=/adapters/support legal=/adapters/legal \
  --max-loras 4 --max-lora-rank 64
```

Each path is a folder in the PEFT format that most training libraries write: `adapter_config.json` and the weights in `adapter_model.safetensors`, or `adapter_model.bin`. A request picks an adapter by its name in the `model` field, and `/v1/models` lists the base model and each adapter. Requests for different adapters can run in the same batch. The manual ran this with Qwen3-0.6B and two public adapters of rank 8 and rank 64, and a chat request to each adapter returned HTTP 200.

### Size the three limits

| Flag | Default | What it limits |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-loras` | 1 | adapters that can run in one batch on the GPU |
| `--max-lora-rank` | 16 | the largest adapter rank the server accepts |
| `--max-cpu-loras` | not set | adapters kept in CPU memory, ready to load |

The default of one adapter per batch is low for a server with many adapters. Requests for a second adapter wait until the batch of the first adapter is done. Raise `--max-loras` to the number of adapters that are busy at the same time. Set `--max-lora-rank` to the largest rank of your adapters and not higher: the server reserves memory for the largest rank it accepts, and the documentation advises against a large default such as 256. Adapters in CPU memory load fast when a request names them, so size `--max-cpu-loras` for the adapters that are warm.

### Load adapters while the server runs

With `VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=True` you can post to `/v1/load_lora_adapter` with a name and a path, and to `/v1/unload_lora_adapter` to remove it. Turn this on only when you trust every caller of the server, because the route loads files from a path that the caller gives.

### What changes elsewhere

- **The prefix cache.** The adapter is part of each block key in vLLM and of the tree key in SGLang. Two adapters never share cached blocks, even for the same prompt. A shared system prompt is cached once per adapter, not once.
- **CUDA graphs.** vLLM captures separate graphs for batches with an adapter. More adapters and more graph sizes add startup time and memory.
- **Names.** Since 0.31 an adapter cannot have the name of a served model.

The manual did not measure the cost of the adapter count or the rank on its hardware.

### Pick the base format with LoRA in mind

The lesson's picking guide says that a 4-bit GPTQ base supports LoRA adapters in vLLM, with the fast Marlin kernels, while the microscaling 4-bit formats did not support LoRA at the start of 2026. For a base model plus many fine-tuned variants, GPTQ is the 4-bit path; AWQ is the pick when there is no LoRA, and FP8 when quality must not move.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Two tenants send the same long system prompt through two different adapters. Does the second request hit the cache? Expected: no; the adapter is part of the block key in vLLM and of the tree key in SGLang, so two adapters never share blocks even for identical tokens.
- **Level 3:** Requests for the second adapter wait although the GPU is idle. Why? Expected: the adapter cap defaults to 1, so only one adapter runs in a batch and requests for another adapter wait until that batch is done; raise it to the number of adapters that are busy at the same time.
