- **Level 3:** Why not set the rank limit to 256 to be safe? Expected: the server reserves memory for the largest rank it accepts, so a high limit takes memory from the KV pool for adapters you do not have; set it to your largest rank.
- **Level 4:** You also want 4-bit weights for the base model. Which format, and what does it rule out? Expected: a GPTQ 4-bit base, because it supports LoRA adapters in vLLM with the Marlin kernels; the microscaling 4-bit formats did not support LoRA at the start of 2026, so they are out until they do.
questions.wrong:
- "One server per adapter is simpler." Each server would hold its own copy of the base model and its own pool; one base with adapters per request shares both, and requests for different adapters can run in the same batch.
- "The default limits are fine." One adapter per batch makes requests for a second adapter wait, and a rank limit of 16 rejects a rank-64 adapter; set both from the adapters you serve.
- "Enable runtime adapter loading so that operators can add adapters without a restart." The load route reads files from a path that the caller gives, so turn it on only when you trust every caller of the server.
- "LoRA is free for the prefix cache because the base model is the same." The adapter changes the keys and values, so it is part of the block key, and two adapters never share cached blocks.

questions.title: One token budget instead of two phases
questions.prompt: Most explanations of continuous batching describe a prefill phase and a decode phase that take turns on the GPU. Describe what the vLLM scheduler does in one step instead. Where does chunked prefill come from in that design, and where do you read the value that controls it?
questions.short: The scheduler asks the same question of every request: how many tokens does it still need to compute? Each step has a budget of tokens, set by `--max-num-batched-tokens`, and the running requests take their next token first. Waiting prompts fill the rest of the budget, so a long prompt is split over several steps, and chunked prefill needs no extra mechanism.
questions.full:
### One question for every request

A new request needs all of its prompt tokens. A running request needs one token, or more with speculative decoding. No prefill phase and no decode phase exist in the code, only a count of tokens still to compute.

### The order inside a step

1. Each running request gets the tokens it needs, up to the budget.
2. Waiting requests are admitted while budget and room remain. `--max-num-seqs` caps the running requests.

A prompt that does not fit the rest of the budget gets a part now and the rest in later steps. That is chunked prefill, and it is on by default because the budget design needs nothing else to support it.

### The default depends on the memory that vLLM reads

| GPU memory that vLLM reads | Budget, `vllm serve` | Budget, `LLM` class | `--max-num-seqs`, both |
|---|---|---|---|
| 160 GiB or more | 16,384 | 16,384 | 1,024 |
| 70 GiB or more, but not an A100 | 8,192 | 16,384 | 1,024 |
| less, or unknown | 2,048 | 8,192 | 256 |

The unified-memory machine in the manual has 121.69 GiB that the CPU and the GPU share, and its log still shows 2,048, the value for a small or unknown GPU. Read the value that your server uses before you change it. At 0.31.0 the log does not print the budget under its own name; find `compile_ranges_endpoints` in the engine config line, and the largest number in that list is the budget.

### Why decode goes first

Running requests come first so that a user who already sees a stream keeps seeing it. A new prompt waits for what is left. A smaller budget gives a smoother stream; a larger one gives a faster first token for long prompts. The small default of 2,048 is a choice for the stream.

### Why one budget

One budget for every kind of work keeps the scheduler simple. Prefix caching only lowers the count of tokens to compute. Speculative decoding only raises the count for a running request. The same loop serves all of them. The cost is that one number decides the balance between the first token and the stream, and no single value suits every workload.

The lesson's toy scheduler uses a fixed 512-token chunk. The real engine has no separate chunk size at 0.31.0: the chunk is what is left of the budget in that step.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Prefix caching is on, and a request with a 2,048-token prompt finds 1,024 tokens in the cache. What does the scheduler count for it? Expected: 1,024 tokens still to compute; the cache only lowers the count, and the same loop serves the request.
- **Level 3:** A server with 121.69 GiB of unified memory logs a budget of 2,048. Why not 8,192? Expected: the default comes from the memory that vLLM reads, and the unified machine reads as small or unknown, so it gets the small value; read compile_ranges_endpoints before you change it.
- **Level 4:** Speculative decoding is on with three draft tokens. How does the budget rule change? Expected: it does not; a running request now needs more than one token per step, so its count rises, and the budget is spent in the same order.
questions.wrong:
- "Chunked prefill is a flag you turn on." It follows from the budget: a prompt that does not fit the rest of the budget gets part now and the rest later, so it is on by default and has no separate mechanism.
- "New prompts go first so that the first token comes fast." Running requests take their tokens first so that a user who sees a stream keeps seeing it; a new prompt waits for the budget that is left.
- "The budget is 2,048 on every GPU." It depends on the memory that vLLM reads: 2,048 below 70 GiB, 8,192 at 70 GiB or more, and 16,384 at 160 GiB or more, and the offline LLM class uses larger values.

questions.title: Why the KV cache is a pool of 16-token blocks
questions.prompt: Explain how vLLM keeps the KV cache in GPU memory. Why does it not give each request its own buffer, how does it recognize a prompt it has seen before, and what happens when the memory runs out?
questions.short: The KV cache is one pool of 16-token blocks, and a request takes blocks one at a time as it grows, mapped by a small block table. A buffer per request wastes memory twice: on length that the request never reaches, and on gaps between requests of different sizes. Each full block gets a hash that is chained with the hash of the block before it, so one hash names a whole prefix, and a new request walks its chain and stops at the first miss. When no block is free, the scheduler preempts the newest request and computes it again later.
questions.full:
### Blocks, not buffers

At startup vLLM splits the cache into blocks of 16 tokens and keeps all of them in one pool. The blocks of a request do not need to be next to each other. A block table maps the token positions of the request to block numbers. The original paper called this PagedAttention, after the way an operating system pages memory.

The lesson gives the size of the waste that this removes. A classic allocator that reserves the full length for every request loses 60 to 80 percent of the memory to fragmentation. With blocks the waste stays under 4 percent. For a 70B model at 8192 tokens, one reserved sequence is about 1.25 GB in BF16, and a request that uses 1500 tokens wastes about 82 percent of it.

### The hash chain

When a block fills, vLLM hashes its tokens together with the hash of the block before it. The chain means that one hash names a whole prefix, not only 16 tokens. The hash also covers the other inputs that change the keys and values: the LoRA adapter, the images in the prompt, and an optional salt for each request. A new request computes the same chain over its prompt and looks each hash up in a map. Every block before the first miss is a hit and needs no compute. Only full blocks are cached, so the tail of a prompt below 16 tokens is always computed.

Since version 0.11 the hash is SHA-256 by default. A faster hash exists, and the documentation warns that a collision could return the wrong blocks or leak data between tenants.

### Eviction

A block that no request uses goes to a free list and keeps its hash. A later request with the same prefix can still use it. When vLLM needs a new block, it takes the head of the free list, the block unused the longest. Only then does the old content go away. So the cache is the pool: no separate cache memory exists, and a busy server keeps fewer old prefixes than an idle one.

### When memory runs out

A running request needs a new block every 16 tokens. If none is free, the scheduler preempts a request. Under the default first-come policy it picks the newest running request, frees all of its blocks, and puts it back at the head of the waiting queue. When the request runs again, vLLM computes its tokens again from the start. Older versions could also copy blocks to CPU memory and back; the current engine only recomputes, because the documentation judges that cheaper. The cost shows as a longer time for the preempted request and in the `vllm:num_preemptions` counter.

### Hybrid models

A model with sliding-window or state-space layers does not keep one entry per token in every layer. Each kind of layer gets its own group with its own page size and its own rule for a hit. The groups share one pool.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Every request starts with the same 25 tokens. How many of them come from the cache? Expected: 16, one full block; the last 9 tokens are computed on every request because only full blocks are cached.
- **Level 3:** Two tenants send the same system prompt. What can one learn about the other, and what field stops it? Expected: they share blocks, so the timing of one tenant can reveal what the other sent; a cache_salt per tenant goes into the hash, so the two never share a block.
- **Level 4:** Under the default policy, which request does vLLM preempt when no block is free, and what does it cost? Expected: the newest running request; all of its blocks are freed, it goes to the head of the waiting queue, and its tokens are computed again from the start, which the preemption counter records.
questions.wrong:
- "vLLM swaps preempted requests to CPU memory." Older versions could; the current engine only recomputes, because the documentation judges the recompute cheaper, and the cost shows in the time of that request and in the preemption counter.
- "The prefix cache has its own memory budget." The cache is the pool; a freed block keeps its hash on the free list until a new block is needed, so a busy server keeps fewer old prefixes than an idle one.
- "A block hash covers only its own 16 tokens." It is chained with the hash of the block before it, so one hash names a whole prefix, and it also covers the adapter, the images and the salt.

questions.title: The two phases of one request
questions.prompt: A user sends a chat request to a serving engine and the answer streams back, slowly at first and then word by word. Describe what the GPU does from the moment the request arrives until the last token. Name the phases, and name the numbers you would put on a dashboard for each of them.
questions.short: A request has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values into the KV cache, so the GPU is busy with math. Decode then writes one token per request per step, and each step reads all the weights to do it, so the GPU waits for memory. Four numbers measure them: TTFT for the wait before the first token, TPOT and ITL for the stream, and output tokens per second for the whole server.
questions.full:
### Prefill

Prefill handles many prompt tokens in one step. The keys and values of every prompt token go into the KV cache. The step does a lot of math for each byte it reads, so it is compute bound. A long prompt makes the first token late.

### Decode

Decode makes one new token for each running request in each step. The step reads all the model weights once to do that, whatever the batch size. The step moves many bytes for little math, so it is memory bound. This is why a bigger batch is almost free per step on a dense model: the weights are read once for all the requests in the step.

### The four numbers

| Number | What it measures | Who feels it |
|---|---|---|
| TTFT | the wait from the request to the first token, mostly queue time and prefill | the person who waits for the answer to start |
| TPOT | the mean time between tokens after the first one | the person who reads a long answer |
| ITL | each gap between two tokens; its P99 shows the worst stalls | the person who sees the stream stop and start |
| Throughput | output tokens per second for all users together | the person who pays for the GPU |

Report the four together. A throughput number alone hides the latency that the users feel.

### What load does to them

The manual measured Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B with vLLM 0.31.0 from one user to 64 users at once:

| Users at once | Median TTFT | Median TPOT | Output tokens per second |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 257 ms | 32.3 ms | 29.5 |
| 64 | 965 ms | 243.8 ms | 239.3 |

With 64 users the server wrote about eight times as many tokens per second. Each user waited almost four times as long for the first token, and each token took about 7.5 times longer. A busy server is cheaper per token and slower for each user. Every tuning choice moves one of these four numbers and costs another.

### One scheduler, not two stages

The engine does not run the two phases as separate stages. In vLLM, each scheduler step has one token budget. Running requests get their next decode token first. The rest of the budget goes to prompt tokens, in chunks. A prefill is only a request with many tokens left to compute.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Which of the four numbers matters most to someone who reads a long answer? Expected: TPOT, the mean gap between tokens, together with the P99 ITL for the worst stalls.
- **Level 2:** Why is decode bound by memory and prefill by math? Expected: a decode step reads every weight to make one token per request, so the bytes moved dominate; a prefill step handles hundreds of prompt tokens per pass, so the math per byte is high.
- **Level 3:** In the manual's run, 64 users got about eight times the output of one user. Why do the cost per token and the wait per user move in opposite directions? Expected: each decode step reads the weights once for all running requests, so more requests share one read; each request then waits for a longer step.
- **Level 4:** The lesson describes a prefill phase and a decode phase. What does the vLLM scheduler have instead? Expected: one token budget per step; running requests take their next token first and prompt chunks fill the rest, so a prefill is a request with many tokens left to compute.
questions.wrong:
- "Throughput is the number to optimize, and the rest follows." Throughput is what the GPU owner pays for; the users feel TTFT and the gaps between tokens, and at 64 users the manual's server wrote eight times the tokens while each user waited about 7.5 times longer per token.
- "Prefill and decode run as two separate stages inside the engine." The vLLM scheduler has one token budget per step; running requests get a decode token first and prompt chunks fill the rest, so the two phases mix in one step.
- "TPOT and ITL are the same number." TPOT is the mean time per output token for one request; ITL is each gap between two tokens, and its P99 shows the stalls that the mean hides.

questions.title: Why one ID at the top of a prompt kills the cache
questions.prompt: Every request to your service starts with the same long system prompt, and the prefix cache is on. The server reports almost no cached tokens, and the first token is slow. Last week a teammate added a request ID to the start of the system prompt for tracing. What happened, and what do you change?
questions.short: The prefix cache matches a prompt from its first token and stops at the first token that differs. A new ID at the start makes every later token a miss, so the server computes the whole prompt again on each request. Move the parts that never change to the front and put the ID after them. Then prove the fix with the cached-token counters.
questions.full:
### Why the position matters

The attention values of each token depend on every token before it. So a cache can reuse a token only when the whole prefix before it is the same. The SGLang radix tree compares tokens from the first one and stops at the first difference. vLLM does the same with blocks of 16 tokens. It caches only full blocks and stops at the first block that differs.

### What it costs

The SGLang manual measured one system prompt of 2,999 tokens in three layouts:

| Layout | Median TTFT | Median cached tokens |
|---|---|---|
| The same prompt every time | 45.1 ms | 2998.0 |
| A random ID at the start | 1255.3 ms | 5 |
| The same ID at the end | 88.2 ms | 2985 |

With the ID at the start, only the 5 tokens before the random digits matched. The first token took 28 times longer. With the ID at the end, the cost was 43 ms.

### The fix

1. Put the parts that never change first: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the fixed instructions.
2. Put the parts that change rarely next, such as the documents of one session.
3. Put the parts that change on every request last: the user question, the time and the request ID.
4. Send the trace ID in a header or a request field, not in the prompt text.

Check the chat template too. Some templates put the date into the system prompt.

### The proof

On vLLM, read `vllm:prefix_cache_hits` and `vllm:prefix_cache_queries` from `/metrics`. The hits divided by the queries is the hit rate. On SGLang, start the server with `--enable-cache-report` and read `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` in each response. A good layout shows almost every prompt token as cached after the first request.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** The hit rate is still low after the fix. What is the next cause to check? Expected: a full pool, because the cache keeps old blocks only until a running request needs the memory.
- **Level 2:** Where in a chat request does a change cost the least? Expected: in the newest message, because the template puts it last, so only that message is computed again.
- **Level 3:** Two tenants send the same system prompt. What is the risk, and what is the control in vLLM? Expected: one tenant can learn from timing what the other sent. Send a different `cache_salt` for each tenant, so that their requests never share blocks.
- **Level 3:** A team tunes the cache tiers and the eviction policy, and the hit rate does not move. What do you check first? Expected: the prompt text, for a value that changes on each request near the start, such as a random hash or a timestamp.
questions.wrong:
- "Give the cache more memory." A bigger pool keeps more blocks, but a prompt that differs at the first tokens has no block to reuse.
- "The cache matches the longest shared part anywhere in the prompt." The cache matches only from the first token, so a shared part after a difference never hits.
- "Turn on hierarchical caching." A second tier stores more prefixes. It cannot match a prefix that is different on every request.

questions.title: Read the GPU clock before the throughput
questions.prompt: Your first sweep on an L4 says that CUDA graphs do nothing: at one user the median per-token time is 103.4 ms with graphs and 103.4 ms without, and the three seeds at that cap spread from 10.0 to 14.9 tokens per second, half the median. What do you check before you report that graphs do nothing?
questions.short: Check the GPU clock and the temperature during the run before you believe either number. The manual's L4 sat at 87 C with software thermal slowdown active and an SM clock of 360 MHz out of 2040 during that sweep, so the server under test was not the cause. A sweep with a cool-down to 72 C and the clock recorded gave 60.16 ms per token at one user against 103.38 hot, and 270.11 against 194.16 tokens per second at a cap of 32: the hot sweep reported up to 28 percent less throughput, with the same command on the same card.
questions.full:
### What the telemetry showed

One driver query during the sweep gave the row: 87 C, 58.36 W of a 72.00 W limit, an SM clock of 360 MHz against a maximum of 2040, the software thermal slowdown bit active, and 100 percent utilization. The L4 is a 72 W card with passive cooling, and the second card in the same chassis ran other work at the same time. The sweep had measured a hot GPU.

### The fix in the method

The sweep script now samples the driver once a second into a file beside each run. Before each run it waits up to 900 s for the GPU to cool below a limit, 65 C by default and 72 C for this chassis. The summary adds the median SM clock, the highest temperature and the share of samples with a thermal slowdown bit to each point. A run under a clock floor is set aside and repeated, up to three times.

The cooled runs are not at full speed either. Their median SM clock was 1,080 to 1,515 MHz of 2,040, and at caps of 1 and 64 the worst seed still had the thermal bit in 41 to 49 percent of its samples. The cool-down removes the worst error, and the recorded clock tells you how much is left.

### Overload heats the card

Under a fixed arrival rate the L4 completed fewer requests the more were offered: 2.01 per second at 4 offered, 1.91 at 8 and 1.62 at 16. The median SM clock fell from 1,320 MHz at 4 offered to 465 MHz at 16, and at 16 the thermal bit was set in 70 percent of the samples. On a passively cooled card overload costs throughput as well as latency. The GB10 showed the same at 16 offered per second: 89 C and 7.3 percent of the samples in thermal slowdown, while its clock stayed at 2,496 MHz up to 4 per second.

### Lock or record

For a comparison of two configs, lock the SM clock with the driver tool, at 900 MHz in the manual's runs, and release the lock after. A lock sets the highest clock and cannot stop the GPU from throttling below it: one run with no speculation fell to 210 MHz under a 900 MHz lock and was set aside. Compare two runs only at the same clock. When the clocks differ by a little, read the ratio between the runs rather than the absolute times, and say the clock in the report.

The manual's position: a benchmark without the clock and the temperature of each run is not evidence.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Which two columns do you add to every result row? Expected: the median SM clock and the highest temperature or the share of samples with the thermal flag, so that a reader can set aside hot runs.
- **Level 3:** You locked the clock at 900 MHz and one run still reports 210 MHz. How? Expected: a lock sets the highest clock and cannot stop the GPU from throttling below it; set that run aside, repeat it after a cool-down, and compare only runs at the same clock.
- **Level 3:** Under an open-loop overload the card finished fewer requests as you offered more. Why? Expected: the queue grew and the card heated, so the clock fell from 1,320 to 465 MHz and 70 percent of the samples showed thermal slowdown at 16 per second; on a passively cooled card overload costs throughput as well as latency.
- **Level 4:** Your chassis cannot cool the card below 72 C. How do you still compare two configs? Expected: run both in one session and alternate them, record the clock for every run, set aside runs under a floor and repeat them, read ratios between runs at similar clocks rather than absolute times, and print the clock next to every number.
questions.wrong:
- "The GPU shows 100 percent utilization, so it runs at full speed." Utilization says the GPU was busy, not how fast; the same card read 100 percent at 360 MHz of 2040 with the thermal flag active.
- "A spread of half the median between seeds is normal noise." On a cool card the bands were inside about 10 percent of their medians; a spread of half the median is a sign of a changing clock, so read the telemetry.
- "A clock lock makes every run comparable." It caps the clock and cannot stop a throttle; a run under the lock fell to 210 MHz and had to be set aside.
- "Record the clock once at the start of the sweep." The clock fell from 1,320 to 465 MHz across one open-loop sweep as the queue grew; sample it once a second during every run and report the median per run.

questions.title: Read three scheduler log lines
questions.prompt:
Here are three lines from two serving engines under load. Read each field and tell me what the server was doing, what the users felt, and which number you would act on.

```text
[2026-10-16 14:01:00] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 7, #new-token: 955, #cached-token: 15102, token usage: 0.05, #running-req: 1, #queue-req: 0, #pending-token: 0, cuda graph: False, input throughput (token/s): 1472.94
[2026-10-16 13:59:09] Decode batch, #running-req: 8, #token: 4075, token usage: 0.02, cuda graph: False, gen throughput (token/s): 98.37, #queue-req: 0
INFO 10-17 22:35:43 [loggers.py:320] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 460.3 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 323.6 tokens/s, Running: 40 reqs, Waiting: 11 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 99.5%, Prefix cache hit rate: 8.7%
```
questions.short: The first line is a prefill batch on SGLang that admitted 7 requests and computed 955 new prompt tokens while 15,102 came from the radix cache, with the pool 5 percent full and nothing waiting: a shared-prefix workload with the cache working. The second is one decode step for 8 running requests at 98.37 tokens per second with an empty queue: a healthy, lightly loaded server. The third is vLLM at a full pool: 40 running, 11 waiting, the cache 99.5 percent used and a hit rate of 8.7 percent, so new requests wait for memory, and the number to act on is the pool.
questions.full:
### The SGLang prefill line, field by field

- `#new-seq` is how many requests this prefill batch admits: 7.
- `#new-token` is how many prompt tokens it computes: 955. `#cached-token` is how many it reused from the radix tree: 15,102. Seven requests shared one long system prompt that an earlier request had computed, so only their questions were new.
- `token usage` is the share of the KV pool held by running requests and cached prefixes together: 0.05, so the pool is nearly empty.
- `#running-req` counts requests that are decoding: 1. `#queue-req` counts requests that wait: 0. `#pending-token` counts tokens of admitted requests that are not yet prefilled: 0.
- `cuda graph` says whether the step replayed a captured graph. False is expected on a platform without graphs, which is where this line came from.
- `input throughput` is the prefill speed of this batch: 1,472.94 tokens per second.

The same benchmark without the radix cache filled three prefill batches of up to 4,096 tokens for eight requests, every one with `#cached-token: 0`. The 4,096 is the chunked prefill size.

### The decode line

SGLang prints one line per prefill batch and one decode line every 40 decode steps by default. This one shows 8 requests decoding together, 4,075 tokens held, 2 percent of the pool used, 98.37 output tokens per second, and no queue. The lines before it in the same run show how the batch formed: one request admitted while 7 waited, then the other 7 admitted together with 3,553 new tokens at 1,914 tokens per second, then all 8 decoding as one batch. Batching the prefill is where the throughput comes from, and the log shows it happen.

### The vLLM stats line

`Running` and `Waiting` are the running and queued requests: 40 and 11. `GPU KV cache usage` is the share of the pool in use: 99.5 percent. `Prefix cache hit rate` is the share of prompt tokens that came from the cache: 8.7 percent. The prompt and generation throughputs say what the engine did in the interval: it prefilled new prompts at 460.3 tokens per second while 40 requests decoded, so each new prefill shared the step with the running streams. In that run, at 64 users on an L4, the median first token was 10,953 ms and the P99 gap between tokens 1,363 ms. The low hit rate is not a fault: the benchmark sent unique prompts, so there was little to share.

### What to act on

- Line 1: nothing. Confirm that the hits persist as the working set grows, because cached prefixes live in the same pool as running requests.
- Line 2: nothing. The server has room; a sweep would tell you how much.
- Line 3: the pool. Grow it with an FP8 cache or FP8 weights, or run fewer users per replica. A cap on the running count would only choose who waits.

Read the pool line at startup as well. On the same card it said `GPU KV cache size: 24,096 tokens, Maximum concurrency for 8,192 tokens per request: 2.94x`, and the 2.94 assumes that every request fills the maximum length.

### What the lines do not show

None of them show the GPU clock, the client that sent the load, or whether the cache was flushed before the run. Those belong in the result next to the lines.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** In the first line, why is the cached count so much larger than the new count? Expected: the 7 requests shared a long system prompt that an earlier request had already computed, so the tree served it and only the questions were new; the no-cache run of the same benchmark showed batches of 4,096 new tokens and zero cached.
- **Level 3:** The hit rate in the third line reads 8.7 percent. Is the cache broken? Expected: no; the random benchmark sends unique prompts, so there is little to share; the hit rate is a property of the prompts, and the number that matters in that line is the pool at 99.5 percent with 11 waiting.
- **Level 3:** What does the token usage field include, and when should it worry you? Expected: the share of the pool held by running requests and by cached prefixes together; near 1.0 the pool is full, new requests queue, and cached prefixes get evicted.
- **Level 4:** Would a cap on running requests help the server in the third line? Expected: no; the pool is full, so a cap only chooses who waits and moves the wait to the first token; grow the pool with an FP8 cache or FP8 weights, or run fewer users per replica.
questions.wrong:
- "A hit rate of 8.7 percent means the prefix cache is misconfigured." Unique prompts have little to share; the hit rate reflects the prompts, and the same engine read far higher on a shared-prefix run.
- "Token usage at 0.05 means the server is almost idle." It means the pool is nearly empty; the GPU can still be busy, as the 1,472.94 prompt tokens per second show; read the running and queue counts for load.
- "cuda graph: False means something is wrong." It says the step did not replay a captured graph, which is expected on a platform without graphs and during a prefill batch; on CUDA, read it on the decode lines.
- "Waiting: 11 is a small queue, so ignore it." With the pool at 99.5 percent every waiting request waits for a running request to finish, and at 64 users on that card the median first token was 10,953 ms; the pool is the limit.

questions.title: Same throughput, two choices at a full pool
questions.prompt: On one L4 with Qwen/Qwen3-8B and the same 24,096-token pool, a closed-loop sweep at 64 users gives vLLM 241 tokens of output per second and SGLang 257, so the engines tie on throughput. Yet the chat team says one of them is unusable at that load and the other is fine. What are they seeing, and which engine do you choose for chat?
questions.short: They are seeing two different choices at a full pool. At 64 users vLLM ran 40 requests and kept 11 waiting with its pool 99.5 percent full, so its first token came 1.7 times sooner, 10,953 against 18,356 ms, but each new prefill shared the step with the running decodes and the P99 gap between tokens was 1,363 ms against 114 on SGLang, which ran 37 requests and kept 27 waiting. For chat, read the P99 ITL next to the first token at your real load and traffic shape, because the two engines pick different sides of that trade by default, and one flag on SGLang moved its side.
questions.full:
### Matched pools, matched clocks

The manual made three choices so that only the engine differed. The vLLM server got `--num-gpu-blocks-override 1506`, 1,506 blocks of 16 tokens, which is 24,096 tokens, while SGLang sized 24,094 tokens for itself. Both ran in one session on one GPU, every run started at 72 C or below, and a run with a median SM clock under 1,000 MHz was set aside and repeated, up to three times. The vLLM server got `--max-model-len 8192`, which every request fits, and its sampler build problem was worked around; the benchmark is greedy, so the sampler does not change the output.

### The closed loop

| Concurrency | Output tok/s, SGLang / vLLM | Median TTFT, SGLang / vLLM | P99 ITL, SGLang / vLLM | Median SM clock, SGLang / vLLM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 13.84 / 13.51 | 185 / 192 ms | 104 / 105 ms | 1,290 / 1,290 MHz |
| 8 | 112.46 / 112.79 | 170 / 253 ms | 71 / 68 ms | 1,485 / 1,470 MHz |
| 16 | 201.13 / 200.90 | 212 / 289 ms | 81 / 80 ms | 1,470 / 1,425 MHz |
| 32 | 271.28 / 273.93 | 2,871 / 1,813 ms | 102 / 619 ms | 1,320 / 1,275 MHz |
| 64 | 256.62 / 241.39 | 18,356 / 10,953 ms | 114 / 1,363 ms | 1,215 / 1,013 MHz |

Up to 32 users the engines were within 3 percent on throughput and within 6 percent on the time per token. Below the point where the pool fills, SGLang gave the first token sooner, 170 against 253 ms at 8 users.

### What the stats lines show

Above that point the engines made different choices. SGLang ran 37 requests and kept 27 waiting, with the pool 92 percent full. vLLM ran 40 requests and kept 11 waiting, filled 99.5 percent of its pool, and prefilled new prompts at 460 tokens per second while it did. More requests started, so their first token came sooner. Each new prefill then shared the step with the running decodes, so the streams stalled. The clock caveat belongs with the last row: even after three tries the vLLM runs at 64 users had a median clock of 1,013 MHz against 1,215, so part of the throughput gap is the card. The 12-times gap in the inter-token tail is too large for a 17 percent clock difference.

### A fixed arrival rate

Up to 2 requests per second the engines tied on throughput, SGLang gave the first token sooner, 284 against 317 ms at 0.5 per second, and vLLM had the shorter time per token, 68 against 74 ms at 1 per second. At 2 per second vLLM served a median of 1.36 requests per second within the latency target and SGLang 0.88, with overlapping seed ranges. From 4 per second both fell behind the arrivals, and the same admission choice appeared: vLLM gave 286.6 against 257.5 tokens per second, 11 percent more, and its P99 time per token was 187 against 127 ms.

### Waves and mixed lengths

With fixed prompt lengths at 16 users, requests arrive in waves, and the engines tied on throughput while vLLM gave the first token sooner, 1,499 against 1,775 ms, and SGLang kept the stream smooth, with a P99 ITL of 81 against 502 ms. With mixed lengths vLLM led by default: 169.6 against 159.6 tokens per second and a P99 ITL of 191 against 363 ms. Then `--enable-mixed-chunk` on SGLang, which puts the running decodes into the prefill batch, closed that gap to 193 against 191 ms, at the cost of a worse P99 ITL with fixed lengths, from 81 to 203 ms.

### Shared prompts

With a shared system prompt both caches hit, and both engines kept the median first token under 500 ms at every shared length. With the cache off SGLang took 14,706 ms and vLLM 13,353 at 4,096 shared tokens. The cache is the result, not the engine.

### The GB10

On the GB10 the two engines gave the same output at 32 and 64 users, and the vLLM P99 ITL was about twice as high, 478 against 220 ms at 32 users.

### How to pick

On this card with unique prompts the choice was mostly a latency decision, and the shape of the traffic picked the winner. When requests arrived together, at a full pool or in waves, SGLang protected the stream and vLLM the first token. With mixed lengths vLLM led by default and one flag removed the lead. Decide on model support, startup time and the hardware you have, then measure your own length mix, and read the P99 ITL next to the first token. Compare engines at matched pools and matched clocks, or not at all.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why did vLLM give the sooner first token and the worse stream at the same throughput? Expected: it admitted more requests, 40 against 37, and filled 99.5 percent of its pool while it prefilled new prompts at 460 tokens per second; each new prefill shared the step with the running decodes, so the streams stalled while the first tokens came sooner.
- **Level 4:** With mixed prompt lengths vLLM led on the stream, and then SGLang tied it. What changed? Expected: the mixed-chunk flag put the running decodes into the prefill batch, so a new prompt no longer stopped the stream; the P99 ITL fell from 363 to 193 ms with mixed lengths, and the cost was a worse P99 ITL with fixed lengths, 81 to 203 ms, because whole waves then shared steps with decodes.
- **Level 4:** A published comparison shows one engine 29 percent ahead. What do you ask before you believe it? Expected: the versions and the date, whether the workload matches yours including the share of repeated prefix, whether the memory budgets and context flags were matched, whether the concurrency passed the decode graph limit, whether the flags were mapped correctly, and who paid for the test.
questions.wrong:
- "They tie on throughput, so pick either." At 64 users the P99 gap between tokens was 1,363 ms on one and 114 on the other at the same output; for chat that is the number the users feel.
- "The engine with the sooner first token is better for chat." It bought the first token with stalls in the stream; the P99 ITL was 12 times higher, and no cap fixed it; read both numbers.
- "The faster engine in the benchmark is faster." Compare only at matched pools and clocks; one published test left one engine at its automatic memory fraction and the other at 0.9 of GPU memory, so the two pools differed.
- "The result transfers to our mixed traffic." The winner changed with the traffic shape: at a full pool and in waves one engine protected the stream, with mixed lengths the other led by default, and one flag removed that lead; measure your own length mix.

questions.title: Why the shared part of the prompt goes first
questions.prompt: Every request to your chat service repeats the same long system prompt, and the engine has prefix caching on by default. What decides whether the next request reuses the work of the last one? How would you lay out the prompt, and how do you show a hit with a number instead of a guess?
questions.short: The cache matches tokens from the first one onward and stops at the first difference, so a hit needs the same tokens in the same order at the start of the prompt. Put the parts that never change first, the parts that change per session next, and the question, the time and any request ID last. Prove the hit from the server: the `cached_tokens` field in the usage block, the `#cached-token` count in the prefill log line, or the prefix cache counters in `/metrics`.
questions.full:
### What a hit saves

On our L4 with Qwen/Qwen3-8B, vLLM 0.31.0 ran 4 groups of 16 prompts at 8 users. The prompts in a group shared a system prompt of the length in the table, then added a 128-token question and asked for 64 tokens back.

| Shared prompt tokens | Median TTFT, cache on | Median TTFT, cache off |
|---|---|---|
| none | 408 ms | 392 ms |
| 256 | 488 ms | 753 ms |
| 1,024 | 396 ms | 1,213 ms |
| 2,048 | 410 ms | 2,550 ms |
| 4,096 | 375 ms | 13,353 ms |

With the cache on, the first token took about 400 ms at every length. Without it, the first token grew with the shared part, because every request computed the whole prompt again. The 1,024 row is the cleanest comparison, because both runs held 1,410 MHz or more; there the cache cut the first token about 3 times and gave 50 percent more output. SGLang on the same card gave the same shape: 479 ms against 14,706 ms at 4,096 shared tokens, with the cache-off run throttled to 930 MHz.

### Why the order decides

The attention values of every token depend on every earlier token. A cache that reused tokens after a change would return wrong answers, so prefix caching is exact by design and unforgiving by the same design. In vLLM the match runs one 16-token block at a time and only full blocks are cached: a shared part of 20 tokens gives one cached block, and the last 4 tokens are computed every time. In SGLang the radix tree matches token by token, and the last prompt token always goes through prefill, because the model needs its logits to sample the first output token. A 2,999-token prompt reported 2,998 cached tokens.

### The order

1. The parts that never change: the system prompt, the tool definitions in a fixed order, the fixed instructions.
2. The parts that change rarely: the documents of one session, the earlier turns, sent unchanged.
3. The parts that change on every request: the user question, the time, the request ID.

Check the chat template too. Some templates put the date into the system prompt. A JSON object whose keys change order is a different token sequence.

### Prove the hit

- vLLM: `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` divided by `vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total` from `/metrics`, and the log line that prints `Prefix cache hit rate`, which read 87.2 percent in the middle of the shared-prefix run.
- SGLang: start with `--enable-cache-report` and read `cached_tokens` in the usage block, read `#cached-token` and `#new-token` in every `Prefill batch` line, or read the `sglang:cache_hit_rate` gauge, which read 0.94 after the shared-prefix benchmark and 0.0 with the cache off.

If the hit rate is low, the prompt order is almost always the cause. A full pool is the next cause, because the cache keeps old blocks only until a running request needs the memory. Routing is the third: with several servers, a request that lands on a server without its prefix misses whatever the prompt looks like, and one report moved its hit rate from 64.7 to 92.1 percent by routing each conversation to the same server.

### Keep tenants apart

Two users with the same prefix share blocks, and the timing of one can reveal what the other sent. A `cache_salt` field per tenant goes into the block key, so different salts never share. The LoRA adapter is part of the key too.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** On vLLM every request starts with the same 20 tokens. How many come from the cache? Expected: 16, one full block; the last 4 are computed each time because only full blocks are cached.
- **Level 3:** The prompt is stable, one server hits well, and the fleet still misses. Name two causes outside the prompt. Expected: a full pool that drops blocks before the next request arrives, and a router that sends a session to a server which never saw its prefix; sticky routing moved one report from 64.7 to 92.1 percent.
- **Level 3:** Why does SGLang report 2,998 cached tokens for a 2,999-token prompt and never 2,999? Expected: the last prompt token always goes through prefill, because the model needs its logits to sample the first output token.
- **Level 4:** A client writes a task-list snapshot at the end of the system prompt and updates it on every turn. What does the tree do? Expected: every update changes the system prompt, so every token after it misses, including the whole history behind it; in the manual's incident that invalidated more than 100,000 tokens per turn, and the fix is to move the snapshot behind the history or into request metadata.
questions.wrong:
- "The cache is on, so repeated prompts hit it." The match is exact from the first token; a timestamp, a request ID or a reordered tool list near the start makes every later block miss, and one random ID at the start matched only 5 tokens of a 3,034-token prompt.
- "Put the user question first so the model reads it first." The question changes on every request, so the shared system prompt behind it never matches; put the fixed part first and the question last.
- "Turn the cache off for a fair benchmark." The cache is on in production, so the test must reset it between runs, not remove it; with it off the first token at 4,096 shared tokens took 13,353 ms on vLLM and 14,706 ms on SGLang.
- "Measure the hit rate from the response time of the client." Read it from the server, in the usage block, the prefill line or the counters; a faster second response can also come from a warmer GPU.

questions.title: Sleep, wake and weight updates for an RL loop
questions.prompt: Your RL trainer shares its GPUs with the vLLM server that generates the rollouts. Between rollout steps the trainer needs the GPU memory back, and after each step the server needs the new weights. What does vLLM give you for this loop, and what can go wrong at the pinned version?
questions.short: vLLM has development-mode routes for the loop: sleep mode frees GPU memory on `/sleep` and takes it back on `/wake_up`, `/pause` and `/resume` stop and restart generation, and a weight transfer runs through `/init_weight_transfer_engine`, `/start_weight_update` and `/finish_weight_update`, over NCCL between GPUs or through CUDA memory handles on one machine. At level 1 the sleep keeps the weights, and at level 2 it drops them too, which suits a step where the trainer sends new weights anyway. Three problems are known at 0.31.0: a level 2 wake does not reload a speculative draft, a level 2 sleep clears calibrated KV scales, and a weight update during sleep stops the engine, so wake first, reload, reset the prefix cache and read the acceptance counters.
questions.full:
### The loop

An RL step has two halves. The rollout half generates answers with the current weights. The training half computes a loss and updates the weights, and the generator needs the new weights before the next rollout. On one set of GPUs the two halves take turns on the same memory, so the generator must give its memory back during training and take it again after.

### The pieces

All of these routes exist only when the server starts with `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`. They free memory, replace weights and run methods on every worker, so never expose a server in this mode outside the network of the trainer; bind it to the local host when you try it by hand.

- **Sleep mode.** Start with `--enable-sleep-mode`. `/sleep?level=1` frees the KV cache and other memory and keeps the weights; level 2 drops the weights too. `--sleep-preserve-parameter-names` keeps frozen weights on the GPU so that they do not move each step. `/is_sleeping` reports the state.
- **Pause and resume.** `/pause` stops new generation and can abort the running requests, wait for them or keep them; `/resume` starts again.
- **Weight updates.** The trainer starts a transfer, calls start, sends the weights, calls finish, and records the version with `/update_weight_version` so that the next rollouts are labelled.
- **Collective calls.** `/collective_rpc` runs a method on every worker, for setup that vLLM does not cover.
- **External launch.** With the external launcher backend, a launcher such as torchrun starts the vLLM workers inside the trainer's processes.

### What the manual saw

A level 1 sleep with Qwen3-0.6B on an L4: each POST returned 200 with an empty body, the sleep took 1.9 s, the GPU memory fell from 14,861 to 4,245 MiB and came back after the wake, and the log line read `Sleep mode freed 10.37 GiB memory`. That is the only timing the manual has; a level 2 sleep and a weight update were not timed.

### What can go wrong at 0.31.0

- A level 2 wake does not reload a speculative draft. The reload covers only the target model, so the target rejects every draft token and decode falls to about the speed with no speculation. The output stays correct and no error appears. The issue is open.
- A level 2 sleep clears calibrated KV scales on some checkpoints with an FP8 cache. The first request after a reload returned NaN logprobs and a wrong first token. The next release fixes this.
- A weight update during sleep segfaults the engine. The API server stays up and every later request fails. The issue is open.

So after each level 2 wake, reload the weights, reset the prefix cache and read the speculative acceptance counters. A reload does not bring back cleared KV scales at 0.31.0; release 0.32.0 fixes that case. Always wake the server before the trainer sends weights.

### The logprob gap

The trainer compares the logprobs that the server returned with the ones it computes itself. They never match exactly, because the kernels differ; a small steady gap is normal, and a growing gap means the weights did not reach the generator. Check which value the server returns first. `--logprobs-mode raw_logprobs`, the default, gives the logprob over the full vocabulary; `processed_logprobs` gives it after the sampling settings change the distribution. With top-p 0.9 the raw mode matched a full-vocabulary reference with a median absolute gap of 0.005, and the processed mode was higher by minus the log of the kept mass, a median shift of about 0.053. Match the mode to the way the trainer scores tokens.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What is the difference between the two sleep levels? Expected: level 1 frees the KV cache and other memory and keeps the weights; level 2 drops the weights too, which suits a step where new weights arrive anyway and costs a reload.
- **Level 3:** After a level 2 wake the output is correct but decode runs as slowly as with no speculation. Why? Expected: the weight reload covers only the target model, so the draft is not reloaded and the target rejects every draft token; no error appears, and the acceptance counters show it.
- **Level 3:** The trainer's logprobs differ from the server's on every token. Bug or not? Expected: a small steady gap is normal because the kernels differ, 0.005 median absolute with raw logprobs; a growing gap means the weights did not arrive, and a constant offset near the log of the kept mass means the server returned processed logprobs under top-p while the trainer scored the full vocabulary.
- **Level 4:** Order the steps of one RL iteration around these routes. Expected: pause or drain generation, sleep, train, wake, then start and finish the weight update and record the version, reset the prefix cache, reload the draft if speculation is on, read the acceptance counters, resume; never send weights while the server sleeps, because that stops the engine.
questions.wrong:
- "Expose the sleep and weight routes on the public port." They exist only in development mode, and they free memory, replace weights and run methods on every worker; keep them on the trainer's network, bound to the local host when you test by hand.
- "Send the new weights while the server sleeps to save time." At 0.31.0 that segfaults the engine; the API server stays up and every later request fails, so always wake before the trainer sends weights.
- "Logprobs from the server and the trainer should match exactly." The kernels differ, so a small steady gap is normal; track it every step and treat a growing gap as a sign that the weights did not reach the generator.
- "A level 2 wake restores the server to its state before the sleep." It reloads the target weights only; the speculative draft is not reloaded and calibrated KV scales were cleared on some checkpoints, so reload, reset the cache and read the acceptance after each level 2 wake, and on 0.31.0 a reload does not bring back the scales.

questions.title: Should the prefill chunk be smaller
questions.prompt: Long prompts make the stream pause for the other users of your SGLang server. A tuning page says to lower `--chunked-prefill-size`, so that decode steps run more often between the pieces of a long prompt. Would you follow it? What did the manual find when it tried, and what would you try instead?
questions.short: Not without a measurement, because the small chunk did not help on either card in the manual's runs. On the GB10 at a low arrival rate a chunk of 1,024 made the P99 ITL worse, 1,977 against 929 ms with the default of 8,192, and at higher rates all chunk sizes tied. I would first try `--enable-mixed-chunk`, which puts the decode tokens into the prefill batch, and measure its trade: on the GB10 it cut the P99 ITL by 15 to 19 percent and at 1 and 2 requests per second it raised the median first token by 49 to 74 percent.
questions.full:
### The rule behind the advice

The scheduler runs a prefill batch whenever it can admit something, and otherwise one decode step. Chunked prefill splits a long prompt into pieces of at most the chunk size, one piece per prefill batch. The default depends on GPU memory: 4,096 on a 22 GB L4 and 8,192 on the GB10. The advice assumes that more pieces give the decode steps more turns.

### What the manual measured

Each run sent 48 prompts of 1,024 to 4,096 tokens with 256 tokens of output, at a Poisson rate of 0.5, 1 or 2 per second, three seeds:

| GPU, model | Chunk | Rate per second | Output tok/s | Median TTFT | P99 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GB10, Qwen3-30B-A3B | 8,192 | 0.5 | 70.1 | 892 ms | 929 ms |
| GB10, Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1,024 | 0.5 | 68.1 | 1,253 ms | 1,977 ms |
| GB10, Qwen3-30B-A3B | 8,192 | 2 | 129.3 | 269 ms | 312 ms |
| GB10, Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1,024 | 2 | 130.1 | 256 ms | 260 ms |
| L4, Qwen3-8B | 4,096 | 0.5 | 44.1 | 36.0 s | 2,579 ms |
| L4, Qwen3-8B | 1,024 | 0.5 | 43.3 | 37.4 s | 2,922 ms |

At 1 and 2 per second on the GB10 the sizes were inside the seed spread of each other. At 0.5 per second the small chunk lost, and the seed ranges did not overlap. On the L4 the workload was more than the card could serve at any rate: output stayed near 44 tokens per second, the first token took 36 to 62 seconds, and the worst gap stayed between 2.5 and 2.9 s with either chunk.

### Why the small chunk lost on a mixture-of-experts model

Each chunk of a prompt loads the chosen expert weights again. A 2025 study of chunked prefill on such models measured up to 39 percent more memory traffic from the extra loads. With a chunk of 1,024 a 4,096-token prompt runs as up to four chunks, and each reads the experts again. The manual did not measure the expert traffic, so this is a reading and not a result.

### Why nothing helped on the L4

Prefill wins whenever the scheduler can admit something. With a full queue, a smaller chunk only adds more prefill turns ahead of the decode steps, and the stream still waits. The manual expects the fix to be more prefill capacity or fewer long prompts per second, and did not test it.

### The mixed chunk

`--enable-mixed-chunk` puts the decode tokens into the prefill batch, so a decode step does not wait for a prefill turn. On the GB10, against a default run of the same day:

| Rate per second | P99 ITL, default / mixed | Median TTFT, default / mixed | Output tok/s, default / mixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 922 / 781 ms | 841 / 910 ms | 70.9 / 72.1 |
| 1 | 219 / 177 ms | 244 / 362 ms | 108.8 / 112.6 |
| 2 | 261 / 221 ms | 238 / 416 ms | 133.2 / 138.1 |

A smoother stream and a slower first token. The P99 ITL fell by 15 to 19 percent, outside the seed spread at 0.5 and 2 per second. The median TTFT rose by 49 to 74 percent at 1 and 2 per second, outside the spread. On the L4 the flag changed the P99 ITL by 5 to 8 percent, inside the spread, because the queue set the pace. The card decided whether you get the trade.

### The other direction fails at startup

With a chunk of 8,192 on the L4 the server exited during graph capture. The pool took the same 24,094 tokens as before, and the prefill graph for 8,192 tokens needed more than the 2.33 GB that remained. The last log line is a PyTorch internal assert that asks for a bug report. The real error is the out-of-memory line two lines above it.

### The same trade in vLLM

vLLM has no separate chunk size. Its token budget plays the same role, and at low load a budget of 16,384 raised the P99 ITL by 39 percent against 2,048 on the GB10. Both engines trade the first token of long prompts against the gaps in the stream, and the best value moves with the load.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why would a small chunk cost more when the model routes each token to a few experts than on a dense model? Expected: each chunk reads the chosen expert weights again, so four chunks can read the experts four times; a dense model reads the same weights once per step either way.
- **Level 3:** On the L4 neither flag moved the stream. Why not? Expected: the card could not keep up with the prompts, so prefill won every turn it could; a smaller chunk only added prefill turns ahead of the decode steps, and the fix is more prefill capacity or fewer long prompts per second.
- **Level 4:** You raise the chunk to 8,192 on the L4 and the server dies at startup with an assert that asks you to report a bug. What happened? Expected: the prefill graph for 8,192 tokens needed more memory than the 2.33 GB that the pool left; the assert is the last line, and the out-of-memory line above it is the cause.
questions.wrong:
- "Smaller chunks always smooth the stream." On the GB10 at 0.5 requests per second the 1,024 chunk raised the P99 ITL from 929 to 1,977 ms, and at higher rates the sizes tied.
- "The mixed chunk is free." It traded a smoother stream for a slower first token: the median TTFT rose 49 to 74 percent at 1 and 2 requests per second on the GB10.
- "The PyTorch assert at startup is a PyTorch bug." The real error is the out-of-memory line two lines above it; the prefill graph for the larger chunk did not fit in the memory that the pool left.
- "A bigger chunk needs no more memory because the pool is the same." The pool stayed at 24,094 tokens, but the captured prefill graph for 8,192 tokens needed more than the 2.33 GB that remained.

questions.title: Speculation won the benchmark and lost in production
questions.prompt: A teammate benchmarked EAGLE-3 on Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 with the random dataset and saw the time per token fall by half at 8 users. In production, with 32 concurrent chat users, the output throughput did not rise and the first token came later. The acceptance length in the log looks fine. What happened?
questions.short: Two things, and the acceptance length hides both. On a 24 GB card the draft weights took pool space: the KV pool fell from 24,094 to 9,951 tokens, about 15 of the 640-token requests, so at 32 users most requests waited for a slot and the median first token went from 2,970 to 8,040 ms. The dataset also matters: at 32 users EAGLE-3 gave 1.6 times the output on GSM8K and code prompts and no more output on the random set or on ShareGPT, because the draft only pays when the GPU has idle time to spend on guesses.
questions.full:
### The L4 sweep

The default server against the EAGLE-3 server with the `Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3` draft, three seeds per point, 512 tokens in and 128 out:

| Concurrency | Default median TPOT | EAGLE-3 median TPOT | Default output tok/s | EAGLE-3 output tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 60.16 ms | 25.61 ms | 13.42 | 31.81 |
| 8 | 66.01 ms | 35.58 ms | 112.62 | 181.55 |
| 32 | 96.18 ms | 43.82 ms | 270.11 | 269.42 |
| 64 | 107.42 ms | 51.50 ms | 250.85 | 245.34 |

The acceptance length was 2.73 to 2.74 tokens per step at every concurrency. Each token came out 1.6 to 2.3 times faster at every load. From concurrency 32 the server delivered no more tokens per second than the default.

### The pool explains the first half

The startup log of the EAGLE-3 server shows the price of a draft on a small card. The target alone had a pool of 24,094 tokens. With the draft loaded, the pool held 9,951 tokens, about 15 requests of 640 tokens, and the draft took nearly 60 percent of the pool. With 15 requests in the pool, the rest waited for a slot. At concurrency 32 the median first token was 8,040 ms with EAGLE-3 and 2,970 ms without it.

The same log line shows `max_running_requests=48`. The speculative handlers set that cap when you do not set it, with one warning that scrolls away before the first request. On the GB10, where the pool had room, the cap was the limit instead: at 64 users throughput was still higher with speculation, 276.32 against 235.38 tokens per second, but the median first token was 7,772 ms against 557 ms, because 16 requests waited behind the 48.

### The dataset explains the second half

The random dataset at this version takes the first turn of ShareGPT conversations and cuts or repeats it to 512 tokens, with the end token ignored. The manual then ran the same L4 sweep on four datasets with the clock locked at 900 MHz and a flush before each run:

| Dataset | Median TPOT at 8 users, default / EAGLE-3 / NGRAM | Output tok/s at 32 users, default / EAGLE-3 / NGRAM |
|---|---|---|
| random | 67.6 to 68.2 / 33.8 to 39.4 / 68.2 to 71.4 ms | 250 to 254 / 239 to 242 / 236 to 250 |
| ShareGPT | 66.4 to 68.6 / 39.5 to 43.1 / 69.5 to 72.4 ms | 281 to 288 / 277 to 283 / 245 to 256 |
| GSM8K | 65.5 / 33.3 to 34.3 / 54.6 to 55.0 ms | 397 / 648 to 660 / 433 to 435 |
| code | 65.9 to 66.4 / 36.8 / 58.2 to 58.8 ms | 365 to 366 / 566 to 581 / 377 to 386 |

EAGLE-3 cut the time per token about in half at 8 users on every dataset, with an acceptance length of 2.35 to 2.78. At 32 users it gave 1.6 times the output on GSM8K and code. On the random set and ShareGPT it gave no more output, and its first token came 2 to 3 times later, because the draft took pool space that the queue needed. NGRAM helped only on GSM8K and code, by about 1.1 to 1.2 times at 8 users, and on the other two sets it was slower, with a P99 ITL of 244 to 779 ms.

### The card and the model decide

The same feature on the GB10 with the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B held its gain at every load, 1.56 to 1.89 times shorter time per token, and still gave 1.17 times the throughput at 64 users. The manual's reading: a dense model reads all its weights per step, so a larger batch already uses the spare compute, while the expert model reads only the experts that the step's tokens chose and the verify pass scores four positions with weights it already read. That is one model and one GPU.

Other teams found the same limits. A benchmark study found that synthetic prompts overstated speculative throughput by 23 percent on average, that the best draft length fell to 1 as the batch grew, and that random token ids left 20 to 30 percent of the experts idle in some layers. A 2025 study of serving benchmarks saw the median TPOT 1.3 times lower and the P99 TPOT 1.16 times higher with speculation, and a later first token because the draft runs its own prefill.

### What to do

1. Read the `KV Cache is allocated` line of the speculative server and compare it with the plain server.
2. Set `--max-running-requests` yourself, from the concurrency where your sweep shows speculation still wins.
3. Benchmark with your own prompts and real output lengths, with `--disable-ignore-eos`, and read `accept len` on them.
4. Compare the P99 ITL and the P99 TTFT, not only the median.
5. Turn speculation on for interactive traffic with a few users per replica; leave it off for batch jobs and for high concurrency on a card where the pool is the limit.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** The log showed 2.73 accepted tokens per step whatever the load. Why did that not predict the throughput? Expected: acceptance measures how well the draft guesses, not whether the GPU has idle time for the guesses or whether the pool has room; the draft took pool space, the queue grew, so each token was faster and the server was not.
- **Level 3:** Which startup lines should the teammate have read? Expected: the allocated KV cache line, 9,951 tokens against 24,094 without the draft, and the running-request cap of 48 that speculation sets when you do not.
- **Level 4:** On the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B the gain held at 64 users. Why would an expert model behave differently? Expected: a dense model reads all its weights per step and a larger batch already uses the spare compute; the expert model reads only the experts that the step's tokens chose, and the verify pass scores four positions with weights it already read, so the gain held at 1.56 times or more; the manual calls this a reading from one model and one GPU.
questions.wrong:
- "The acceptance length is fine, so speculation is working." It measures the draft's guesses, not the server; on the L4 each token came 1.6 to 2.3 times faster at every load and the server delivered no more tokens per second from 32 users.
- "Random prompts are real text, so the benchmark is realistic." The random set cuts or repeats the first turn of ShareGPT conversations to 512 tokens with the end token ignored; on GSM8K and code prompts speculation gave 1.6 times the output at 32 users, and on ShareGPT it gave none.
- "Raise --max-running-requests to let more users in." On the L4 the pool held about 15 requests, so a higher cap changes nothing; the pool was the limit, and the draft took nearly 60 percent of it.
- "Use NGRAM instead, it needs no draft weights." It helped only on GSM8K and code, by about 1.1 to 1.2 times at 8 users, and on the other two sets it was slower with a P99 ITL of 244 to 779 ms.

questions.title: Temperature zero gave two different answers
questions.prompt: You run the same evaluation twice at temperature 0 on a serving engine and the scores differ. You send one failing prompt alone and get one answer, then send it inside a busy batch and get another. Nothing in the request changed. Explain what did change, and what a seed can and cannot fix.
questions.short: The batch changed the arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative, and the kernels split their sums by the batch size, so the same request adds its numbers in a different order in a batch of 3 than in a batch of 30; a change in the last bit can flip the top logit, and every later token then follows a different text. The prefix cache does the same, because a request that reuses cached blocks runs a different prefill path, and so does the dtype. A seed fixes only the random draws of sampling, so it is not enough: offline, run the engine in one process with the same order; online, use the batch-invariant mode and pay its speed cost.
questions.full:
### Four things that change one request

- **The batch.** Matrix multiplies, softmax and norms split their sums into tiles, and many kernels pick the split from the batch size.
- **The schedule.** In a multiprocess server, the timing of requests decides which batch each one joins.
- **The prefix cache.** A request that reuses cached blocks computes its prompt in a different way than a request with no hit.
- **The dtype.** BF16 and FP16 round each number differently, so the same model writes different text in the two.

The vLLM seed defaults to 0 and cannot be unset, because speculative decoding needs every worker to sample the same tokens. So a seed is always there, and it is not enough by itself.

### What the manual counted

Greedy outputs of Qwen3-0.6B, 32 ShareGPT questions after one shared system prompt of about 170 tokens, 128 output tokens, compared token by token between two runs. The number in brackets is the median position of the first token that differs:

| Comparison | SGLang | vLLM |
|---|---|---|
| flushed repeat against fresh | 0 of 32 | 0 of 32 |
| cache off against cache off | 0 of 32 | 0 of 32 |
| fresh against warm cache | 21 of 32 (45) | 11 of 32 (57) |
| cache on against cache off | 25 of 32 (26) | 21 of 32 (48) |

At one user and the same cache state, the text repeated exactly. A warm cache changed 21 of 32 outputs on SGLang and 11 of 32 on vLLM. At 64 users sent at once, two runs with the cache off still differed, in 27 of 64 outputs on SGLang and 50 of 64 on vLLM: the batch alone changed most outputs. BF16 against FP16 at one user changed 48 of 64 outputs on vLLM and 51 of 64 on SGLang for the 0.6B model, and 56 and 57 of 64 for Qwen3-1.7B.

The SGLang probe on the GB10 makes the point in one prompt. Sent five times alone and five times inside a batch of 16 at temperature 0, the default server wrote two texts, which parted after 238 characters. The first request alone had computed its prompt from nothing; the four later ones found it in the radix cache. With deterministic mode on, all ten requests wrote the same text.

### What fixes it

| Case | Fix | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Offline evals with the `LLM` class | `VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=0`, the same seed, the same prompts in the same order | the engine runs in your process, so the schedule repeats |
| A live server | `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, or `--enable-deterministic-inference` on SGLang | slower kernels for every request |
| Greedy evals that must match exactly | greedy sampling plus one of the two above | as above |

Every fix also needs the same hardware, the same engine version and the same settings. On SGLang the flag replaces the matrix, softmax, norm and batched-multiply operators with batch-invariant kernels, forces the plain sampler, fixes the all-reduce order under tensor parallelism, accepts only some attention backends, turns the radix cache off unless the backend supports it, and gives every request without a `sampling_seed` the seed 42.

### How to test it

Run the same eval twice and compare the outputs token by token, not only the score. Flush the prefix cache or restart the server before each probe. If the outputs differ, take one prompt that differs and run it alone twice. If the two answers match when alone, and the batched probe started from the same cache state, the batch causes the difference. SGLang ships a test that sends one prompt in random batch sizes and counts distinct outputs, with modes for a single prompt, shared prefixes and cached against uncached prefill.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Which comparisons in the manual's table gave the same text every time? Expected: a repeat after a cache flush against a fresh run, and a repeat with the cache off against the cache off, both 0 of 32 changed on both engines.
- **Level 3:** Why can a warm prefix cache change a greedy answer when the model and the prompt are the same? Expected: a request that reuses cached blocks computes its prompt in a different path than a full prefill, so the logits differ in their last bits, and one changed token changes the rest; it changed 21 of 32 outputs on SGLang and 11 of 32 on vLLM.
- **Level 4:** Under load two cache-off runs still differed. What does that say about the fix? Expected: the batch alone changed most outputs, 50 of 64 on vLLM, so a cache reset is enough only at one user; a live server needs batch-invariant kernels, and the manual did not test that mode at that load.
questions.wrong:
- "Temperature 0 makes the output deterministic." Greedy picks the top logit, and the batch changes the logits in their last bits; the GB10 server gave two texts for one prompt at temperature 0 with nothing in the request changed.
- "Set a seed and the outputs match." The seed only fixes the random draws; the vLLM seed defaults to 0 and cannot be unset, and the outputs still changed with the batch and the cache.
- "Flush the cache before each run and you are done." At one user that was enough, 0 of 32 changed; at 64 users two runs with the cache off still differed in 50 of 64 outputs, because the batch changed the sums.
- "Switch to FP16 for exact results." BF16 and FP16 round differently, so the same model writes different text in the two dtypes, 48 of 64 outputs for the 0.6B model; keep one dtype between runs you compare.

questions.title: Choose tensor, pipeline or data parallelism
questions.prompt: You have a model that does not fit on one GPU, or you need more throughput than one GPU gives. Walk me through how you choose between tensor, pipeline and data parallelism, and what each one costs in communication.
questions.short: Ask three questions. If the model fits on one GPU with room for the KV cache you need, use data parallelism, one full copy per GPU, and the output grows with the copies. If it does not fit, split it: tensor parallelism inside one machine when the GPUs have a fast link and the GPU count divides the attention heads, and pipeline parallelism when they do not or when the model needs more than one machine. Tensor parallelism talks after every layer, pipeline parallelism once per stage boundary, and data parallelism not at all between copies.
questions.full:
### Three questions

| Question | If yes | If no |
|---|---|---|
| Does the model fit on one GPU, with room for the KV cache you need? | Data parallelism: one copy per GPU, `--data-parallel-size N`. | Split the model; the next question decides where. |
| Does the split model fit inside one machine? | Keep the split inside the machine; the next question picks the layout. | Add pipeline parallelism across machines. |
| Do the GPUs have NVLink, and does the GPU count divide the model evenly? | Tensor parallelism, `--tensor-parallel-size N`. | Pipeline parallelism inside the machine, `--pipeline-parallel-size N`. |

Across machines: set the pipeline size to the number of machines and the tensor size to the GPUs in each machine. The tensor size must divide the attention-head count. If the GPUs in a machine do not divide it, use a tensor size of 1 and put the whole GPU count into the pipeline size.

### What each layout costs

| Layout | What it splits | Communication | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tensor | each layer across GPUs | after every layer, so it needs a fast link | a model too big for one GPU, inside one machine |
| Pipeline | the layers into stages | once per stage boundary | a model too big for one machine, or GPUs without a fast link |
| Data | nothing, each GPU holds a copy | none between copies | more output from a model that fits |
| Expert | the experts of a mixture-of-experts model | before and after the expert layers | large expert models |

Tensor parallelism also splits the KV cache, so each GPU has more room for it. When the weights fill most of one GPU, two GPUs can hold several times the pool of one. The exception is a model with multi-head latent attention: it stores one compressed latent per token that cannot be split across heads, so every tensor-parallel rank keeps the full cache and more ranks add no tokens. Attention data parallelism answers that case.

### Check the link

Tensor parallelism sends data after every layer. On GPUs joined only by PCIe, such as two L4s in one host, that traffic can cost more than the split saves. The vLLM documentation suggests pipeline parallelism on such a machine, because it sends data only at stage boundaries, and it also accepts a GPU count that does not divide the model evenly. The manual did not run either layout on its two L4s, so measure them against each other before you pick.

### Start a second machine

Run the collective test script on both machines first. When the network and the drivers work, each process prints its success lines. Then start the server with a launcher that spans the machines, and start the API on one machine only. The traffic between the machines is not encrypted and can run code on the other side, so keep it on a private network.

### Count the processes

With data parallelism vLLM starts one engine core per copy and one coordinator that keeps them in step. With tensor parallelism it starts one worker per GPU under one engine core. In SGLang the world size is `--tp-size` times `--pp-size`, and `--dp-size` copies get a controller that sends each request to one copy, round robin by default. That controller does not look at pools or queues. On the manual's two L4s, where one card was shared and its copy had a pool of 2,925 tokens against 24,094, the pair served less than one card at every load.

### Give a tensor group whole GPUs

Before SGLang loads weights for a tensor group, each rank measures its free memory and the group keeps the smallest value. If that value is under 90 percent of the local free memory, the server stops. On the shared pair the second card had 18.28 GB free against the 19.53 GB that the check required, so `--tp-size 2` refused to start, and no flag turns the check off. Every rank holds the same share of weights and the same pool, so the smallest card sets the size for all of them.

### Very long prompts

For prompts of hundreds of thousands of tokens, vLLM can split one sequence across GPUs with context parallelism. Use it when one long request is the problem, not when many short ones are.
