- **Level 2:** Two GPUs in one host joined by PCIe only, and the model fits on one. What do you run? Expected: data parallelism, two full copies, because nothing moves between copies; tensor parallelism would pay after every layer over the slow link.
- **Level 3:** The model needs two machines of 8 GPUs. How do you set the sizes, and what do you check first? Expected: pipeline size 2 for the machines and tensor size 8 inside each, with 8 dividing the attention heads; run the collective test on both machines first and keep the traffic on a private network, because it is not encrypted.
- **Level 3:** Tensor parallelism on two GPUs where one is shared with another job. What does SGLang do at startup? Expected: it measures free memory on each rank, keeps the smallest, and stops if that is under 90 percent of the local free memory, because every rank holds the same share and pool; give the group whole GPUs.
- **Level 4:** Why does tensor parallelism add no KV capacity when the attention keeps one latent per token? Expected: that attention stores one compressed latent per token that cannot be split across heads, so every rank keeps the full cache; attention data parallelism gives each group its own requests and cache, so capacity grows with the groups.
questions.wrong:
- "Tensor parallelism is the default way to use more GPUs." It is the way to make a model fit; when the model fits, data parallelism adds output with no traffic between copies, and tensor parallelism over PCIe can cost more than it saves.
- "More copies always mean more throughput." Only when every copy has about the same pool; a pair where one copy had an eighth of the pool served less than one card, because the round-robin controller fed it half the requests.
- "Pipeline parallelism is only for several machines." Inside one machine it is the choice when the GPUs lack a fast link or when the GPU count does not divide the model evenly.
- "Any GPU count works with tensor parallelism." The size must divide the attention-head count of the model; otherwise use a tensor size of 1 and put the whole count into the pipeline size.

questions.title: Two clients, two numbers, one server
questions.prompt: Two engineers benchmark the same server on the same day and report numbers that differ by a few percent. Both used standard benchmark clients. Before you look at the server, what about the clients could explain the gap, and what rules would you set for the team?
questions.short: The client is part of the measurement. On one vLLM server the SGLang client read a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher and an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower than the vLLM client, the two clients sent different random prompts, and temperature 0.7 raised the time per token by 10 to 13 percent at one user against temperature 0. The rules: one client, one temperature, one prompt length distribution with the range ratio stated, a flush and a new seed per run, the clock recorded, and all of that written next to every number.
questions.full:
### Three clients on one server

The manual ran the SGLang client, `vllm bench serve` and its Rust version against one vLLM server with Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, with a cache reset before every run and the clients alternated over two rounds. Output tokens per second at 64 users:

| Temperature | SGLang client | vllm bench | vllm bench, Rust |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 359, 348 | 379, 377 | 371, 365 |
| 0.7 | 331, 343 | 360, 363 | 356, 353 |

The two vLLM clients agreed within the noise at 1, 16 and 64 users. The SGLang client read a slower server: a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher, and at 16 and 64 users an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower. The two clients send different prompt tokens from their random datasets, so part of a small gap can come from the prompts. Temperature 0.7 raised the median time per token over temperature 0 by 10 to 13 percent at one user and 3 to 6 percent at 16 and 64 users.

### Four defaults that change the result

The SGLang client makes choices before it measures anything:

| Setting | Default | What it does to the result |
|---|---|---|
| `--random-range-ratio` | 0.0 | each length is drawn from 1 to the length you asked for, so the average prompt is about half of it |
| `ignore_eos` | on | every request generates exactly the output length you asked for |
| `--request-rate` | inf | all requests are sent at time 0, and only the concurrency cap holds them back |
| `--warmup-requests` | 1 | one request runs before the clock starts |

The first row is the trap. With the default ratio, an input length of 512 gives an average prompt near 256 tokens, and the report says 512. Pass 1.0 or write the length distribution next to the result. With 1.0, 32 prompts of 512 tokens give an input total of 16384 in the report.

### Fixed lengths form waves

With the ratio at 1.0 every request has the same length, so requests that start together finish together and their replacements arrive together. At 16 users on the L4, fixed lengths gave a median time to first token of 1,996 ms and a P99 ITL of 82 ms; mixed lengths gave 291 ms and 300 ms. The two settings measure two different servers. Fixed lengths measure bursts, with a slow first token and smooth tokens. Mixed lengths measure steady traffic, with a fast first token and stalls in the stream. Keep 1.0 to compare two builds, and run your real length mix before you set a latency target.

### The client's own queue

The SGLang client sends every request from one Python process. A 2026 study found that such a client adds its own queue at high request rates and then reports a first token and a time per token higher than the server gave. Before you trust a number at a high rate, compare one client process with two processes that each send half the rate. The lesson names the same trap for a general load tester: tokenization under the interpreter lock in the client inflates the reported inter-token latency, and one prompt sent in a loop hits the prefix cache on almost every request and inflates the throughput.

### Hand-written scripts

One report measured 13 tokens per second for a large model on eight GPUs against 60 from a hosted API. The script counted words split on spaces and included the first-token time in the rate. A word is not a token, and TTFT is not decode time. Use the benchmark client, which counts tokens and keeps TTFT and TPOT apart.

### The rules

1. One client, one version, named in every result.
2. One temperature, named in every result.
3. `--random-range-ratio 1.0`, or the length distribution written down.
4. A flush and a new seed before every run, and the cached tokens recorded.
5. The GPU clock recorded and the hot runs set aside.
6. Throughput reported only together with the median and P99 TTFT and TPOT at the same cap.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the default range ratio describe half the work? Expected: each length is drawn from 1 to the length asked, so the average prompt is about half of it; with 1.0 every prompt has the full length and the input token total in the report confirms it.
- **Level 3:** Fixed lengths gave a late first token and a steady stream, mixed lengths the opposite. Which do you use? Expected: fixed lengths to compare two builds, because they repeat exactly; your real length mix before you set a latency target, because the two shapes measure two different servers.
- **Level 3:** A teammate's hand-written timing loop reads 13 tokens per second where a hosted API reads 60. What is wrong with the loop? Expected: it counted words split on spaces and included the first-token time in the rate; a word is not a token and TTFT is not decode time, so use the benchmark client.
- **Level 4:** At 16 requests per second the client reports a first token you do not believe. How do you check the client itself? Expected: a single-process client adds its own queue at high rates; run two client processes that each send half the rate and compare, and record the CPU use of the client.
questions.wrong:
- "Both are standard clients, so the numbers are comparable." On one server the SGLang client read 3 to 10 percent higher first-token times and 2 to 8 percent lower throughput than the vLLM client; a gap of a few percent can come from the client alone.
- "Temperature does not change speed." Temperature 0.7 raised the median time per token 10 to 13 percent at one user and 3 to 6 percent at 16 and 64 users over temperature 0.
- "Set the input length to 512 and the prompts are 512 tokens." With the default range ratio of 0.0 the average prompt is about 256 tokens; pass 1.0 or state the distribution.
- "A load tester that handles HTTP handles model traffic." A generic tool sends one prompt in a loop, which hits the prefix cache almost every time, and it does not read the token gaps of a stream; use a client that samples prompt lengths and counts tokens.

questions.title: What determinism costs a live server
questions.prompt: Your evaluation team wants bit-identical outputs from the live server and asks you to enable batch invariance for all traffic. What does it change, what does it cost, and what would you say?
questions.short: The mode replaces the kernels that split their sums by the batch size with kernels that keep one reduction order, so one request gives the same logits alone and in a batch. It costs speed, most at low concurrency: on our L4 the small model paid 2.4 times the time per token at one user and 1.4 times at 32, and Qwen3-8B paid 1.4 times at 8 users with 27 percent less output. I would turn it on for evaluation and rollout servers and leave it off for production traffic, after I measured the cost at the concurrency we serve, because on SGLang with the default backend it also turns prefix caching off.
questions.full:
### What the mode switches

On vLLM, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` needs a GPU of compute capability 8.0 or higher, which includes the L4 and the GB10, and it turns off speed features that change the order of the sums, such as custom all-reduce with tensor parallelism. At 0.31.0 it is in beta.

On SGLang, `--enable-deterministic-inference` replaces the matrix multiply, the log-softmax, the mean, the RMS norm and the batched multiply with batch-invariant kernels, forces the plain sampling backend, sets the all-reduce to a tree so that tensor-parallel sums add in a fixed order, accepts only some attention backends, turns the radix cache off unless the backend is one that supports it, and gives every request without a `sampling_seed` the seed 42. The cache rule matters most: with the default backend on the GB10 the log said that the radix cache is not compatible, so every repeated prefix paid its full prefill again. On the L4 the mode picked a different backend that keeps the cache on.

### What the manual measured

vLLM on the L4 with the clock locked at 900 MHz, Qwen3-0.6B, runs in the order default, batch-invariant, default again, two seeds each with a cache reset before each run:

| Users | Median TPOT, default / batch-invariant | Output tok/s, default / batch-invariant |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6.9 / 16.9 ms (2.4x) | 140.6 / 58.7 (58% lower) |
| 8 | 9.9 / 18.2 ms (1.8x) | 755 / 420 (44% lower) |
| 32 | 18.8 / 25.9 ms (1.4x) | 1,565 / 1,154 (26% lower) |

On Qwen3-8B at 8 users the time per token was 1.4 times longer and the output 27 percent lower; at 32 users 1.3 times and 23 percent. The relative cost fell as more users shared each step, and it was larger on the small model.

SGLang on the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B, one run per server at concurrency 8: output fell from 78.92 to 64.83 tokens per second, 18 percent, and the median time per token rose from 97.30 to 117.43 ms. The radix cache was off in that run, so a workload with shared prefixes pays more than this number shows.

### What other teams measured

A post on nondeterminism ran 1,000 Qwen3-8B requests on vLLM in 26 s by default, 55 s with batch-invariant kernels, and 42 s with a better attention kernel. A 2026 study measured batch-invariant kernels at more than twice the latency and up to 74 percent less throughput. A verification study found that the modes of both engines gave different logits under some changes in execution, such as prompt chunking and KV cache reuse. The manual did not measure these itself.

### What the mode does not cover

At 0.31.0 a vLLM model that picks its own attention backend skips the check, so its output can still depend on the batch; the next release checks every attention layer, and a fix for expert models with data, tensor and expert parallelism under compile is not in it. On SGLang a hybrid state-space model was reported as not batch-invariant, some newer architectures are not yet supported, a sliding-window kernel gave several greedy outputs in prefix mode with the issue still open, and one speculative algorithm gave different text after a restart because kernel autotuning picked different tactics on each start.

### What I would say

Use the mode where identical bits are the product: reinforcement learning rollouts and evaluations that must reproduce. Keep production traffic on the default kernels, where prefix caching and faster kernels are worth more than identical bits. Measure the cost at the concurrency you serve, not at one point, and test the exact setup: model, attention backend, parallel layout, chunk size and cache setting. Flush the cache between two runs you compare, and keep the dtype the same.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why did the relative cost shrink at higher concurrency? Expected: the invariant kernels give up the fast splits that an idle GPU would use, and that loss is a larger share of a small step; with more rows per step the fixed order costs a smaller share, 1.4 times at 32 users against 2.4 at one.
- **Level 3:** On SGLang the 18 percent understates the cost for a chat workload. Why? Expected: with the default attention backend deterministic mode turns the radix cache off, so every repeated prefix pays its full prefill again; pick a backend that keeps the cache where the GPU supports it.
- **Level 4:** Two servers both run the mode and still give different greedy text for one prompt. Name three causes. Expected: different hardware or engine version; a model path the mode does not cover, such as an attention layer that picks its own backend or a hybrid state-space layer; and kernel autotuning that picked different tactics on each start.
questions.wrong:
- "The mode has no cost when the GPU is idle." The cost is largest at low concurrency, 2.4 times the time per token at one user on the small model, because the invariant kernels give up the fast splits that an idle GPU would use.
- "Turn it on for production, because correctness comes first." Production traffic gains more from prefix caching and fast kernels than from identical bits; the manual's position is to use the mode for rollouts and evaluations and to measure the cost at the concurrency you serve.
- "The flag covers every model." At 0.31.0 a model that picks its own attention backend skips the check, hybrid state-space layers are not covered, and a fix for expert models under compile is not in the next release; test the exact setup.
- "The seed 42 makes sampled requests reproducible." It makes every request without a sampling_seed draw the same random numbers, which is reproducible and also identical across users; set a sampling_seed per request that must reproduce.

questions.title: A larger token budget at low load
questions.prompt: A teammate proposes `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384` so that long prompts get their first token sooner. The server runs a model with mixture-of-experts layers on one card. Requests arrive at about half a request per second, with prompts between 1,024 and 4,096 tokens. What do you expect to change, and what would you measure before you accept the change?
questions.short: A larger budget lets a long prompt finish its prefill in fewer steps, but each of those steps takes longer, and every running stream waits for it. At low load I expect a faster first token and a worse P99 ITL, and I would measure both with several seeds at the real request rate. On our GB10 at 0.5 requests per second, 16,384 raised the P99 ITL from 574 to 798 ms, while the first-token gain did not clear the seed spread.
questions.full:
### What the manual measured

Budgets of 2,048 and 16,384 tokens on the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B, requests at a fixed rate, three seeds per point, each request asking for 64 to 256 tokens:

| Requests per second | Budget | Median TTFT | Median TPOT | P99 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 2,048 | 1,145 ms | 149.3 ms | 574 ms |
| 0.5 | 16,384 | 906 ms | 139.4 ms | 798 ms |
| 1 | 2,048 | 454 ms | 156.5 ms | 405 ms |
| 1 | 16,384 | 477 ms | 156.9 ms | 395 ms |
| 2 | 2,048 | 560 ms | 205.5 ms | 587 ms |
| 2 | 16,384 | 595 ms | 205.1 ms | 586 ms |

At 0.5 requests per second the larger budget raised the P99 ITL by 39 percent, and the seed ranges did not overlap. The first token came sooner, but the seed ranges of the first token overlapped. So the cost is clear and the gain is not confirmed. At 1 and 2 requests per second the two budgets gave the same numbers within the seed ranges. All runs held a median clock of 2,398 to 2,411 MHz, so the clock does not explain any row.

### Why the effect fades with the rate

At a higher rate more requests share each step. One long prompt then fills a smaller share of the budget, and how it is chunked matters less. The result is narrow: two budgets, three low rates, one model, one machine. The P-PAS paper found that no single fixed budget was best at every load: a large budget won at low prefill pressure, a small one when several prefills competed with running streams.

### An open result

The median first token at 0.5 requests per second was slower than at 1 request per second for both budgets. All three seeds at 0.5 were above 900 ms with the 2,048 budget, and all three at 1 were below 600 ms. One slow seed does not explain it. The manual did not find the cause and says so.

### How to decide

1. Read the budget that your server uses. The run with no flag matched 2,048 on this machine.
2. If the P99 ITL is too high and long prompts arrive, lower the budget.
3. If the first token of long prompts is too slow and the P99 ITL has room, raise it.
4. Measure at your real request rate, and again when your load changes.

`--long-prefill-token-threshold` caps the tokens that one long prompt gets in a step when other requests wait. It is off by default and the manual did not test it.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** At the two higher rates the budgets tied. Why does the difference vanish as the rate rises? Expected: more requests share each step, so one long prompt fills a smaller share of the budget and its chunking matters less.
- **Level 3:** Both budgets gave a later first token at the lowest rate than at the next rate up. How do you report that? Expected: all three seeds agreed, so it is not one slow seed; the cause was not found, so it stays an open result and no rule is built on it.
- **Level 4:** Is there one budget that wins at every load? Expected: no; a large budget wins when prefill pressure is low and a small one when several prefills compete with streams, so the value must move with the load.
questions.wrong:
- "A larger budget is free because the GPU has spare compute at low load." Each step with a bigger chunk takes longer and every running stream waits for it; the P99 ITL rose 39 percent at 0.5 requests per second.
- "Set the budget once from the GPU size and leave it." The best value moved with the request rate in these runs, so measure at your real rate and again when the load changes.
- "The drop from 1,145 to 906 ms proves the first-token gain." The seed ranges of the first token overlapped, so the cost is confirmed and the gain is not.

questions.title: Two data-parallel copies, less output than one card
questions.prompt: You add a second L4 to an SGLang server with `--dp-size 2` and expect about twice the throughput. The sweep shows less than one card gave: at 64 users the pair peaks at 64 tokens per second and falls to 42, and the P99 first token is 391 seconds against 33.4 on one card. Both copies loaded the weights without an error. What do you check, and what went wrong?
questions.short: Read the `KV Cache is allocated` line of every DP rank before you trust the sum. On that pair the second card ran two pods of another team, so its copy had 3.17 GB free after the weights against 6.59 GB and a pool of 2,925 tokens against 24,094, an eighth of the first. The round-robin controller does not look at pools, so it sent every second request to the small copy, where 4 ran and 59 waited, while the large copy held one to three requests and used 2 to 7 percent of its pool.
questions.full:
### The two pools

The startup lines of the two ranks tell the story before the first request:

- `DP0` loaded the weights in 3.61 s and had 6.59 GB left; its pool was 24,094 tokens.
- `DP1` loaded the same 15.28 GB of weights in 3.73 s and had 3.17 GB left, because two pods of 1,746 MiB each held the rest; its pool was 2,925 tokens. Four requests of 640 tokens fill it.

The decode lines at 64 running requests show the result. `DP1` ran 4 requests at a token usage of 0.82 to 0.87 with 59 in its queue. `DP0` ran one to three requests at a usage of 0.02 to 0.07 with an empty queue.

### Why the client could not help

The benchmark keeps 64 requests open at a time. Round robin alternates requests between the copies without a look at pools or queues. At 64 users, 63 requests sat on the small copy, 4 running and 59 waiting. The client could not send the large copy more work until the small copy gave a slot back.

### What it cost

One L4 reached 270 tokens per second. The pair peaked at 64 and fell to 42 as its clock fell: it ran at 765 and 675 MHz at 32 and 64 users, under the manual's clock floor, while the single card ran at 1,320 and 1,080 MHz, so part of the loss is the clock. At 64 users the median P99 first token of three seeds was 33.4 seconds on one card and 391 seconds on the pair. Up to 4 users the pair was already 16 to 41 percent slower for a reason the manual did not isolate, and at one user it took 79.6 ms per token against 60.2 at a higher clock. With a fixed arrival rate the pair completed at most 0.21 requests per second inside the latency target, against 0.96 for one card.

### Route by tokens

`--load-balance-method total_tokens` sends each request to the copy that holds the fewest tokens. On the same uneven pair it gave 114.7 tokens per second at 64 users, against 41.7 with round robin and 250.9 on one L4. At 8 users it gave 92.1 against 64.2 and 112.6. The median first token at 64 users fell from 4,763 to 3,977 ms. That run had a median clock of 1,020 MHz against 675 in the round-robin run, so part of the gain is the card. A large gain over round robin, and still a loss against one card.

### Tensor parallelism would have refused

`--tp-size 2` on the same pair stopped two seconds after the collective library started. Before it loads weights, each rank measures its free memory and the group keeps the smallest value. If that value is under 90 percent of the local free memory, the server stops. The shared card had 18.28 GB free against the 19.53 GB that the check required. Each rank of a tensor group holds the same share of weights and the same pool, so the smallest card sets the size for all. `--dp-size 2` has no such check, because each copy sizes its own pool, so it started and lost.

### The rule

Add capacity with copies only when every copy has about the same pool. Give a group whole GPUs on a shared machine. Check the `#tokens` line of each DP rank before you count on the sum. The other fix, two separate servers behind a gateway with weights, the manual did not measure.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why did the large copy sit almost idle while 59 requests waited? Expected: the benchmark is a closed loop with 64 open requests, round robin put half of them on the small copy, and the client could not send new work to the large copy until the small copy returned a slot.
- **Level 3:** Why did a tensor split refuse the same pair while the data-parallel pair started? Expected: tensor parallelism checks that every rank has at least 90 percent of the local free memory, because every rank holds the same share and pool, and the shared card had 18.28 GB against the 19.53 GB required; data parallelism sizes each copy's pool on its own and has no such check.
- **Level 4:** Routing by total tokens lifted the pair to 114.7 at 64 users. Is the problem solved? Expected: no; one card alone gave 250.9, the token-routed run also had a higher clock than the round-robin run so part of the gain is the card, and the fix is equal pools, with whole GPUs for each copy or separate servers behind a gateway with weights.
questions.wrong:
- "Both copies loaded, so the second card is fine." The weights need 15.28 GB on each card; the pool is sized from what is left, and the shared card had 3.17 GB left against 6.59, an eighth of the pool.
- "The controller balances load, so a slow copy gets fewer requests." The default round robin does not look at pools or queues; it alternated requests, so 63 of 64 open requests ended on the small copy.
- "The pair is slower because of the clock, so run it again when the card is cool." The pair did run under the clock floor at 32 and 64 users, but it was already 16 to 41 percent slower up to 4 users, and the log shows 59 requests waiting on one copy; the pool explains the shape and the clock explains part of the size.

questions.title: When prefill-decode disaggregation pays
questions.prompt: Your chat users see a smooth stream until someone pastes a long document, and then every stream pauses while the server prefills it. A colleague proposes prefill-decode disaggregation: separate prefill servers and decode servers. When does that split pay, what does it not do, and how would you decide?
questions.short: Split prefill from decode when the measured problem is the tail of the inter-token latency and long prompts cause it, because a prefill server then never shares a step with a stream. It does not raise throughput: the documentation says so, it costs a KV transfer for every request plus more servers and a router, and a 2025 study found that even the tail gain depends on the load and on the path that moves the cache. Decide with a measurement: one server first, then copies behind a gateway, and the split last, compared with the same GPUs run as plain servers at your real load.
questions.full:
### What it solves and what it does not

On one server a long prompt shares each step with the running streams, and every stream waits a little longer for its next token. Chunked prefill makes the pause shorter but cannot remove it. Two kinds of server remove it: a prefill server computes the prompt and builds its KV cache, and a decode server receives that cache and writes the answer.

The vLLM documentation says that disaggregated prefill does not raise throughput. It gives control over the first token and the stream as two separate numbers, and it controls the tail of the inter-token latency. Even that gain is a condition, not a default: the study that compared split servers with servers that run both stages found that it depends on the request load and on the path that moves the cache.

### How the cache moves

In SGLang the gateway starts every exchange. It picks one prefill server and one decode server, adds the bootstrap host and port of the prefill server and a random 63-bit room number, and sends the same request to both. The decode server reserves KV slots and publishes their addresses. The prefill server runs a normal prefill and writes the KV pages straight into those slots, a one-sided RDMA write with the default transfer backend, or over TCP on a cluster without RDMA cards. The decode server sees the transfer finish and adds the request to its running batch. Every transfer moves through bootstrapping, waiting, transferring and success, and any stage can fail. The bootstrap port defaults to 8998, both timeouts to 300 seconds, and the transfer queue count to 4.

In vLLM each server gets a KV connector and a role, `kv_producer` or `kv_consumer`, and the common connector needs a library that the wheel does not install, pinned at 1.4.1. A router sends each request to the prefill server first, reads the transfer parameters from its response, and sends the request to the decode server with them. If a transfer fails, the default policy fails the request; `kv_load_failure_policy` set to `recompute` computes the prompt again on the decode server instead.

Never send a request straight to a role server. The scheduler asserts that a bootstrap room exists and tells you to use the router.

### The order to decide

1. Measure TTFT and inter-token latency on one server with a benchmark that mixes long and short prompts.
2. Add data-parallel copies behind a gateway, and measure again.
3. Split only when the inter-token tail still rises when long prompts arrive, and compare the split with the same GPUs as plain servers at your real load.

### Size the two sides

Long prompts with short answers need more prefill capacity. Short prompts with long answers need more decode capacity. One test on eight GPUs found that at high concurrency one prefill server for three decode servers won every metric, while at low concurrency three to one and two to two gave a better first token. It shows the direction, not your ratio. Measure the first token and the stream on each side and move one server at a time.

### What went wrong for other teams

- A pair with one prefill and one decode server had a higher first token than one plain server with the same split of GPUs. An old transfer library was the cause, and an upgrade fixed it. Without the single-server baseline nobody would have known.
- At 64 concurrent requests one setup logged many bootstrap failures and `Aborted by AbortReq` on the prefill side, while 4 to 7 concurrent requests worked. The router's timeout for the prefill client was too short, and a later fix lengthened it. The rule: an abort means the client or the router aborted, so check timeouts before you suspect the transfer.
- With the overlap scheduler on, one deployment saw throughput rise about 10 percent and the first token get much worse, because the KV transfer waited for the next kernel launch; their fix was a flag that the manual could not find in the pinned version.

### What to watch after the split

The bootstrap-failed and transfer-failed counters must stay flat. The transfer latency and speed gauges show the cost of each move. The decode pre-allocation and transfer queue gauges show requests that wait for memory or for a transfer. In every benchmark, read the retokenized output tokens before the throughput.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** On the same GPUs, the split pair's first token arrives later than the plain server's. What do you suspect first? Expected: the transfer path, an old transfer library or a router timeout; one incident fixed it with an upgrade, and only the single-server baseline showed that the split made it worse.
- **Level 3:** Prefill logs aborts at a load of 64 users and works at 4 to 7. Where is the fault? Expected: in the router or client timeouts, which aborted requests that were still running, not in the transfer; a later fix lengthened the router timeout.
- **Level 4:** How do you pick the ratio of prefill to decode servers? Expected: from your prompt and answer lengths and your concurrency; long prompts with short answers need more prefill and the reverse more decode; one test found one prefill for three decode servers won at high concurrency and three to one or two to two gave a better first token at low concurrency, so measure both sides and move one server at a time.
questions.wrong:
- "Disaggregation raises throughput." The documentation says it does not; it gives control over the first token and the stream as two numbers and costs a KV transfer per request and more servers.
- "Send requests straight to the decode server to skip the router." The scheduler asserts that a bootstrap room exists and tells you to send requests to the router; the room is how the two servers find each other's half of one request.
- "A failed transfer falls back to a normal prefill." The vLLM default policy fails the request; set the failure policy to recompute if you want the decode server to compute the prompt again.
- "Chunked prefill already solves this." It makes the pause shorter but cannot remove it, because the chunk still shares the step with the running decodes; the split removes the sharing at the cost of a transfer and a second set of failures.
